cards.x: Start by installing the add-on, then use its Content Installer to add the plants, textures, and biomes. Most of this setup takes place in Blender's Preferences, available from Edit > Preferences.

1. Open Edit, choose Preferences..., and select Get Extensions. 2. Click the arrow in the upper-right corner and choose Install from Disk.... 3. Select the downloaded ScatterFlow .zip file. Do not extract it first. 4. Select Add-ons, search for ScatterFlow, and make sure its checkbox is enabled. Expand the entry to view its version and preferences. 5. Close Preferences. In the 3D viewport, press N to open the sidebar, then select the ScatterFlow Professional tab. Requires Blender 5.2 or newer. To use ScatterFlow Nano, use the ScatterFlow build of Blender. Extract its folder and launch blender.exe; no installation is required. This build is in beta, so keep backups of your .blend files. On Windows, the first launch may display “Windows protected your PC.” For the ScatterFlow build you downloaded, the launch options are More info, then Run anyway.

Plants, rocks, textures, and biomes are distributed separately from the add-on. Install them using the Content Installer at the top of ScatterFlow's preferences. ScatterFlow_Pro_ContentPack.part1.rar and ScatterFlow_Pro_ContentPack.part2.rar contain the plants, rocks, and textures. They form one archive split into two parts, approximately 5.5 GB in total. ScatterFlow_ProBiomes.zip contains the biomes. 1. Download all three files into the same folder. Leave them compressed; the installer extracts them. 2. Set Content Library Folder to the location where you want to store the installed content. Allow approximately 6 GB for the extracted files. The installer remains disabled until you select a folder. 3. Click Install Content Files and select the downloads. For the two-part archive, select either part; the installer finds the other in the same folder. You can select the archive and the biomes zip together. Supported content file formats are .zip, .rar, .gscatter, and .blend. 4. Follow the installation progress in the status bar. Extracting the main archive can take several minutes. Blender remains usable during installation, and Esc cancels the operation. 5. Check the installation list. Each entry changes from Not installed to a checkmark and Installed when ready. Once ScatterFlow Assets & Textures and ScatterFlow Biomes are installed, the biomes appear in the Biome Browser. The same list also reports installed GScatter packs and compatibility asset libraries. RAR extraction requires 7-Zip or WinRAR. Blender cannot extract .rar files directly. The installer uses either application if it is installed. If neither is available, it reports Extracting multi-part .rar archives needs 7-Zip (free, 7-zip.org) or WinRAR. Install 7-Zip from 7-zip.org, then run Install Content Files again.

cards.t: When the content does not install
cards.x: “The first part ScatterFlow_Pro_ContentPack.part1.rar is missing.” or “Part ... of the archive is missing.” Keep both parts in the same folder with their original filenames. Download any missing part again. “... could not be extracted”: an archive part may be damaged or incomplete. Compare its size with the download page and download the affected part again. Not enough disk space. Extraction takes place inside the Content Library Folder and requires approximately 6 GB. Downloads stored on the same drive occupy another 5.5 GB until you delete them after installation. Assets & Textures still shows Not installed. Run Install Content Files with the original downloads. Manually copying an extracted folder into the library does not register the content as installed. Reinstalling the same files preserves existing content and adds missing files, making it useful for repairing an incomplete installation.
Expand Settings below the Content Installer to access the remaining preferences.

Density 1Scale 1Random Scale onRandom Rotation onAlign to Surface offBounding Box off These settings apply to new scatter layers only. Changing them does not affect existing layers. Density and Scale set the initial Density and Uniform Scale values. Random Scale, Random Rotation, and Align to Surface determine whether those features are enabled when a layer is created. Bounding Box enables Optimized Mesh for new layers, displaying instances as boxes in the viewport. Use it when setting up scenes with heavy assets. Click Save Preferences in the lower-left corner if Blender is not configured to save preferences automatically.

Automatic Scene Switch Detection refreshes the System List when you switch scenes. It is the same option as Auto Refresh in the layer menu. This feature is experimental. Enable it when you regularly work across multiple scenes and need the layer list to update automatically.

The Export and Megascans panels contain settings for game engine export and Megascans installation. See the Megascans page for the installation workflow. Debug Logging writes additional information to Blender's console. Leave it disabled unless support asks you to enable it.

cards.t: Content pack and the Asset Browser
cards.s: Content pack and the Asset Browser
cards.pt: Content pack and the Asset Browser
cards.x: The ScatterFlow content pack includes plants, rocks, props, and effects. Its assets are used by the bundled biomes, but you can also add them individually through Blender's Asset Browser. After installing the content, register its folder as an asset library so Blender can display it.

cards.pt: Content pack and the Asset Browser
cards.x: Register the library once in Blender's Asset Libraries preferences. This is a separate step from installing the files with ScatterFlow's Content Installer.

cards.pt: Content pack and the Asset Browser
cards.x: 1. Open Edit > Preferences and select Asset Libraries. 2. Click + beside the library list and select the ScatterFlow_Pro_ContentPack folder. Select the folder itself, not a file inside it. 3. Select the new library entry and check that its Path ends with ScatterFlow_Pro_ContentPack. 4. Set Import Method to Append. Assets added to a scene will become editable copies in that file. 5. Close Preferences. The library is now available in the menu at the upper left of any Asset Browser. Update the path after moving the library. If the assets disappear after you move the folder, return to these preferences and set Path to its new location.

cards.pt: Content pack and the Asset Browser
cards.x: Open an Asset Browser. You can change an existing editor, such as the Timeline, to an Asset Browser and resize it to show more assets. Choose ScatterFlow_Pro_ContentPack from the library menu. The catalogs organize the assets into the following groups: Foliage: Bushes, Cactus, Grass, Ground Debris, Moss, Mushrooms, Plants, Rocks, Sticks, and Trees. Ivy: leaves, flowers, and presets for the Ivy tools. Trash & Debris: barrels, boxes, construction debris, bins, food and drink, glass, set pieces, and loose trash. Water, Weather, and Atmosphere: water presets, rain, snow, wind, and effects such as dust, embers, and falling leaves. Select a catalog to filter the assets, or expand its arrow to browse subcategories. Use Search to find assets by name, such as “fern.” Initial loading may take longer. The library is large, and asset previews may take a moment to appear the first time you open it.

cards.pt: Content pack and the Asset Browser
cards.x: Drag an asset into the 3D viewport and release it over the target surface. The asset snaps to the surface beneath the cursor. Most assets contain several variations rather than a single object. For example, Ferns includes four ferns, while Desert Rocks2 includes sixteen rocks. The variations arrive in a row, grouped in a collection named after the asset. Reposition them or remove variations you do not need. Materials are included. Switch to Material Preview or Rendered shading to see the textures. For manually placed props, use Randomize Transform to vary their appearance and Snap to Ground to position them on the terrain.

cards.t: From an asset to a scatter layer
cards.pt: Content pack and the Asset Browser
cards.x: An imported asset's collection of variations can be used directly as the source for a scatter layer. 1. Drag the asset into the scene. 2. Choose an Emitter in the ScatterFlow panel and click + to add a layer. 3. Under Instances, set Type to Multiple Instances and select the asset's collection, such as Ferns. 4. Increase Density / m² to populate the surface. The layer uses the variations in the collection. You can now adjust the layer with the Scatter tab's controls, including Scale, Rotation, masks, and Wind. Supported content pack materials also respond to the Materials section's season, snow, and dryness settings. After setup, you can hide the original objects or move them out of view. Keep them in the file: the scatter layer uses them as its source objects.

ScatterFlow extracts Megascans downloads, imports their models, builds materials from the included textures, and saves the results in the Megascans_SF asset library. Once installed, these assets are available through the Asset Browser in any Blender file.
Choose a library location before installing your first asset.

1. Open Edit > Preferences, select Add-ons, and expand ScatterFlow. 2. Expand Settings, then Megascans. 3. Set Folder to the location where you want to store Megascans assets. Allow room for both the extracted source files and the finished Blender assets. 4. Click Register / Refresh Asset Library. ScatterFlow creates the folder if needed and registers it as Megascans_SF in Blender. See The settings, one by one for details about each option.
The Megascans panel contains two settings and one library registration button.

Sets the location for all installed Megascans content. Until you choose a folder, the panel displays Choose a folder before installing Megascans assets. and disables the button below it. The folder contains three items: Assets: one .blend file per asset, organized by type, such as 3D Assets, 3D Plants, and Surfaces. These files appear in the Asset Browser. SourceFiles: the extracted downloads, including their models and full-resolution textures. Asset materials reference textures here, so do not delete this folder. blender_assets.cats.txt: the catalog definitions used to organize the Asset Browser. A single extracted download can occupy several hundred megabytes. To relocate the library, move the entire folder, update Folder, and click Register / Refresh Asset Library.

Default Off Some Megascans downloads include multiple levels of detail (LODs). LOD0 is the most detailed model; LOD1, LOD2, and subsequent versions use progressively fewer polygons. Off: installs only the most detailed version of each model. Use this when you need the full-detail asset for Blender rendering. Omitting the additional LODs keeps the installed files smaller than installing all versions. On: installs every available LOD into the same asset. Its description lists the included versions, for example Included LODs: LOD0, LOD1, LOD2. Use this when you also need lighter models for distant scattering or game engine use. This option applies during installation. Changing it does not alter existing assets; reinstall a download to change which LODs it includes.

Registers the selected folder with Blender and refreshes its library setup: 1. Creates the folder if it does not exist. 2. Adds Megascans_SF under Edit > Preferences > Asset Libraries with the import method set to Append. Assets added to a scene become editable copies. 3. Creates the Megascans catalogs: 3D Assets, 3D Plants, Surfaces, Decals, Atlases, Imperfections, and Brushes. 4. Refreshes open Asset Browsers and saves the preferences so the library remains registered after restarting Blender. When complete, the status bar displays Megascans_SF ready and the library location. Installing an asset also performs these steps. Use the button during initial setup, after changing Folder, or when the library is missing from the Asset Browser.

1. Open an Asset Browser. You can change an existing editor, such as the Timeline, to an Asset Browser. 2. Click Install Megascans on the right side of its header. 3. Select a downloaded Megascans .zip and confirm. You can select multiple zip files, or browse into an already extracted Megascans folder. 4. Choose Megascans_SF from the library menu. The installed asset appears with a preview in its matching Megascans catalog. Asset not visible? Click the refresh arrows beside the library menu.

Drag an asset from the Asset Browser into the 3D viewport. It becomes an ordinary object that you can move, edit, or scatter. Its material is already configured with the available colour, roughness, normal, and displacement textures. Inspect the connections in the Shader Editor, or use Material Preview or Rendered shading to view the result. Assets are appended rather than linked, so editing an imported object does not change the library copy. To scatter an object, select it in a layer's Instances section.

The installer reads the download's metadata to identify its asset type and select the matching catalog. 3D assets and 3D plants become model assets. A download containing several variations becomes one asset containing all of them, with a description such as Contains 3 variations. Dragging it into a scene imports every variation, ready to use together in a scatter layer. Surfaces, decals, imperfections, atlases, and brushes contain textures rather than models and become material assets. Drag one onto an object to apply the material. Supported model formats are FBX, OBJ, glTF, USD, Alembic, PLY, and STL. Supported texture formats are JPG, PNG, TIFF, EXR, TGA, BMP, WebP, and HDR.

Materials are assembled from textures identified by filename. Supported inputs include colour, ambient occlusion, roughness, gloss, metalness, specular, normal, bump, displacement, opacity, and translucency. Ambient occlusion is multiplied into the colour, and gloss maps are converted to roughness. The highest-resolution version of each texture is used. Opacity maps configure cutout materials for assets such as leaves and grass. Displacement maps set the material to Displacement and Bump: in Cycles, displacement moves the surface when the mesh has sufficient geometry; otherwise, it contributes bump detail.

Reinstalling an asset replaces its .blend file and its extracted copy in SourceFiles. Use this to change the included LODs or repair an asset. Objects already imported into Blender scenes are separate copies and are not replaced by the reinstall.

“Choose an Asset Library folder first.” Set Folder in the Megascans preferences. See Install location. “Select a Megascans ZIP, or browse into a Megascans folder.” Select the zip files themselves, or open an extracted Megascans folder and click Install Megascans without selecting an individual file. “No supported mesh or Megascans texture maps were found in that source.” The selected source contains no recognized model or texture files. Check that it is a supported Megascans download. “Installed 2 of 3 source(s). 1 failed; see System Console.” One or more downloads failed during a batch installation. Open Window > Toggle System Console to see the reason for each failure.
An emitter is the object a scatter setup belongs to, usually a terrain. Select an emitter to access the layer list and the rest of the Scatter tab.

Choose an object in the Emitter field, or use the eyedropper to select one in the viewport. The System List and layer settings appear below it. Each emitter has its own layer list. Use separate emitters to organize scattering across multiple terrains, such as a meadow and a hill. Switching emitters changes the list you are editing. Layers assigned to other emitters remain active in the scene.

A layer defines one scatter setup: the objects to place, their density, and the masks and other settings that control them. The System List displays the current emitter's layers. Settings below the list apply to the selected layer.

Click + beside the System List. A new layer named ScatterSystem is created and selected. Choose its source objects in the Instances section. Double-click the layer name to rename it. Use descriptive names such as Rocks to identify its contents. New layers use the default density, scale, and rotation settings from the add-on preferences. Object Mode required. Switch Blender to Object Mode before adding a layer.

The monitor icon controls a layer's viewport visibility. The camera icon controls its render visibility. Hide heavy layers in the viewport while leaving them enabled for rendering to keep the scene easier to work with. The colour swatch on the left is an organizational label. Change it to distinguish related layers; it does not affect their appearance in the scene.

Select a layer, open the arrow menu below the list buttons, and choose Duplicate Layer. The copy retains all settings and receives the original name with _Copy appended. The copied layer initially places instances at the same positions as the original. Change its Seed to create a different arrangement, or choose different source objects to reuse the layout with another asset.
Select a layer, click −, and confirm. This removes the layer and its scattered instances, but leaves the source objects unchanged.
Click a row to edit that layer. The settings below the System List update to match your selection. Use the up and down arrows to reorder layers and keep related entries together.

These options are available in the same arrow menu as Duplicate Layer. Refresh List synchronizes the System List with the current scene. Use it if the list still shows layers from a previous scene after switching scenes. Auto Refresh updates the list automatically when the scene changes.
A group organizes multiple layers in one folder. It also lets you hide, duplicate, or adjust those layers together.

cards.t: Create a group and fill it
cards.x: Click the folder button beside the System List to create an empty group. Double-click its name to rename it, for example Forest. To add a layer, select it and click + on the group's row. The layer appears indented beneath the group. Adding a layer to a group does not change its individual settings.

cards.t: The buttons on a group row
cards.x: The triangle expands or collapses the group's contents. The eye shows or hides every layer in the group in both the viewport and renders. The − on a grouped layer's row removes that layer from the group. The group remains even if it becomes empty. The duplicate icon copies the group and all its layers. Deleting a group preserves its layers. Select the group and click the System List's − button. Only the folder is removed; its layers return to the top level of the list.

Select the group itself to display Group Scattering in place of the layer's Scattering section. These controls affect every layer in the group while preserving each layer's own Density and Seed values.

Default 100% Multiplies every layer's density by the same percentage. At 100%, densities are unchanged; 50% halves them, and 200% doubles them. Use this to thin or fill out an entire biome while preserving the proportions of trees, bushes, rocks, and other layers. For example, 25% produces a sparse version of the group, while 250% makes it substantially denser.

Default 0 Adds an offset to each layer's seed, changing the group's arrangement without replacing its individual seed values. Layers retain their different patterns. Return the offset to 0 to restore the arrangement defined by the layers' own seeds.

Default ProceduralGroup Spread 5.00 Switches all layers in the group between Procedural and Manual scattering. In Manual mode, Start Placing paints the group's layers together. Use it to place a mix of trees, bushes, and rocks with one stroke. Group Spread controls how far apart the layers place their instances around the brush. Lower values create a tighter band; higher values spread the layers further apart. See Manual Mode for the individual brush controls.
Selecting a group also displays group versions of other supported sections, including Group Surface and Group Scale. Their controls are covered on the corresponding feature pages.
Surface, Instances, and Scattering are the first three sections below the System List. All three apply to the selected layer.
Choose the geometry that receives the layer's instances. This can be the emitter itself, another object, or a collection of objects.

Default Emitter Object Emitter Object scatters on the current emitter. Its name appears below the setting as a read-only reference. Single Surface scatters on another object selected in the field below. Use it to place a layer on a specific surface, such as one boulder, without changing its emitter. Multiple Surfaces scatters on all objects in the selected collection. For example, select a collection of boulders to cover every rock while leaving the surrounding terrain clear. The layer remains in its emitter's System List regardless of which surface it uses. Collection missing from the picker? Multiple Surfaces lists collections directly beneath the Scene Collection. Move a nested collection to that level to make it available.
Choose the objects the layer places on its surface.

Scatters one source object. Select it in the field below Type, or use the eyedropper. Replacing the source object preserves the scatter positions. Use this to compare a tree, rock, or bush in the same layout without changing the distribution.

Scatters a mix of objects from a collection. Set Type to Multiple Instances and select the collection; each scatter point uses one of its objects. Add or remove objects in the collection to change the available mix. The layer updates automatically.
Control the placement method, instance density, and spacing.

Default Procedural Procedural distributes instances across the surface according to settings such as Density and masks. Changing a setting updates the scatter automatically. Manual starts with an empty layer and lets you place instances with brushes. It replaces Density and the Factor buttons with a Manual Mode section containing Start Placing. See Manual Mode for the available brushes. Use Procedural for coverage that should respond to changes in your setup. Use Manual for deliberate placement, such as a hero tree or a carefully arranged path edge. Both approaches can be combined by creating one layer of each with the same source objects. Switching modes preserves manual placements. Returning to Procedural restores the automatic scatter. Switching back to Manual restores your hand-placed instances.

Sets the number of instances per square metre of surface. A value of 1 on a 40 m × 40 m surface produces approximately 1,600 instances before masks remove any. Use higher densities for small plants and lower densities for trees. Adjust Density to compare sparse and dense coverage.

Default 0 Changes the random arrangement without changing the number of instances. Enter a value or click the dice button to choose a random seed. Different seeds help prevent separate layers from placing instances at matching positions.

Default 2.00 Controls the amount used by the four Density adjustment buttons: multiply, divide, add, and subtract. With Factor set to 2, * doubles Density and / halves it. The + and − buttons add or subtract the Factor value itself. For sparse layers, use a smaller Factor, such as 0.1, before adding or subtracting.

Default offMinimum Distance 0 m Enforces minimum spacing between instances in the same layer. Enable the option and set Minimum Distance to the closest allowed spacing. Instances that violate the spacing are removed. Increasing Minimum Distance therefore reduces the number of instances, and at larger values spacing becomes the limiting factor rather than Density. This setting only checks the current layer. To control spacing between different layers, use Ecosystem.

Use Manual Mode for placements that need direct control, such as a hero tree, vegetation along a path, or the edge of a clearing. Set the layer's Scattering Type to Manual to display the Manual Mode section. See Scattering Type for a comparison with Procedural mode.

cards.t: Start Placing and the mode dials
cards.x: Click Start Placing to display the numbered brush dials on the left of the viewport. A shortcut card appears beneath them. Select a brush by clicking its dial or pressing its number, 1–9. The selected dial remains visible with its settings, while the other dials collapse. Click the active dial again to display the full brush list. No instances are placed until a brush is selected. Press Esc, Enter, or the right mouse button to leave Manual Mode. Your placements remain on the layer.
Control which source objects the placement brushes can use.

The list shows the objects assigned in the layer's Instances section, along with their polygon counts. Disable an object's checkbox to exclude it from new placements. For example, disable rocks and bushes to paint only the trees in a mixed collection. All enables every object; None disables them all. Enable at least one object. Start Placing cannot begin when every object is disabled.

Hold Ctrl and drag to erase instances. The brush ring turns red while erasing. There are two exceptions: with Scale, Ctrl shrinks instances; with Attract, it pushes them away. Hold F and move the mouse horizontally to adjust the brush size. This changes the same value as the Radius dial. Viewport navigation with the middle mouse button and mouse wheel remains available while painting.

Drag a dial horizontally to change its value. Hold Shift for finer adjustments, or use the mouse wheel while hovering over the dial. Ctrl+click or double-click resets a dial to its default. Click an on/off dial to toggle it. Every brush has a Radius control. The default is 2.0, except for Precision, which uses 0.7.

Density 1Delay 1.00Surface Rotation on Places random instances within the brush area as you drag. Density sets how many instances each step of the stroke adds. Increase it for denser coverage. Delay controls the distance between placement steps, not the time between them. Lower values create a continuous band; higher values produce separated clusters. Surface Rotation aligns new instances to the slope beneath them. Disable it to keep them upright.

Scale 1.00Mesh Preview on Places one instance at a time. A transparent preview follows the cursor. Press and drag to position the instance, then release to place it. Scale sets the size of the next instance. Swap Preview, or F8, switches to another enabled object from the layer. This is available when the layer uses a collection with more than one object enabled in Scatter Manager. Mesh Preview toggles the transparent object preview. When disabled, the cursor shows a simple ring.

Density 1Delay 1.00Surface Rotation on Places instances like Area, but rotates each one to face along the brush stroke. Use it for directional arrangements such as fences, logs, hedges, or crop rows. Density, Delay, and Surface Rotation work as they do for Area. Their values are stored separately for Align.
These brushes modify existing hand-placed instances on the active layer. They do not affect instances on other layers.

Adjust Normals off Press over a group of instances and drag to move them across the surface. The brush picks up the instances inside its radius at the start of the drag. Set Radius large enough to include the entire group before moving it. Adjust Normals realigns moved instances to the slope at their new position.

Scale Speed 0.05 Hold the mouse button over instances to enlarge them. Hold Ctrl to shrink them instead. Scaling continues while the button is held, so use short presses for controlled adjustments. Scale Speed controls how quickly instances grow or shrink.

Jitter 0.10 Adds random tilt to instances under the brush. The effect builds while the brush remains over them. Use it to break up an arrangement that looks too uniform. Jitter sets the amount of tilt added at each step.

Probability 0.10Min Distance 0.70 Thins crowded areas by removing instances that are too close to their neighbours. Min Distance sets the target spacing. Instances closer together than this may be removed. Probability sets the chance of removing each eligible instance on a brush pass. Lower values thin the layer gradually over repeated strokes; higher values remove more at once.

Pull Speed 0.03Adjust Normals off Hold the mouse button to pull instances inside the brush toward the cursor. Holding longer forms a tighter cluster; eventually, all affected instances can converge on the same point. Hold Ctrl to push instances away instead. They move toward the edge of the brush and stop there, making this useful for opening a clearing. Increase Radius to affect a larger area. Pull Speed controls how quickly instances move. Adjust Normals realigns instances to the surface as they move.

Rotate Speed 0.015 Leans instances in the direction of the brush stroke. Use it to flatten grass or give trees a directional, wind-blown appearance. Rotate Speed controls how strongly each brush movement changes their lean.
Select a group and set its Type to Manual to paint its layers together. Group painting adds a Group Spread control for the spacing between layers around the brush. See Group Scattering for details.
The Scale section combines three independently enabled controls: overall scale, per-axis scale, and random variation. Their values multiply together, so you can use them at the same time.

Default on, 1.0 Scales every instance by the same factor. A value of 1 preserves the source object's size, 2 doubles it, and 0.5 halves it. Disable Uniform Scale to remove its effect without losing the stored value. The starting value for new layers is set in the add-on preferences.

Default off, 1 / 1 / 1 Scales instances independently along X, Y, and Z. Increase Z to make objects taller, or adjust X and Y to change their width. Use it to create variations such as taller grass or flatter rocks without modifying the source mesh.

New layers onMin 0.6Max 1Seed 0 Assigns each instance a random scale between Min and Max. New layers start with a range of 0.6 to 1 times the source size. Lower Min for stronger variation; values near 0 produce many very small instances. Set Max above 1 to allow instances larger than the source object. Whether new layers start with Random Scale enabled is set by the Random Scale preference; see Defaults. Seed changes which instances receive each size without changing the range.
When a group is selected, Group Scale replaces the layer's Scale section. Its Uniform Scale applies to every layer in the group.
Rotation combines a fixed rotation, alignment to the surface, and random variation. These controls are available for individual layers, not groups.

Default off, 0° / 0° / 0° Rotates every instance by the same amount around X, Y, and Z. Z changes its heading, while X and Y add tilt. Use it to correct the orientation of a source object or lean an entire layer in one direction.

Default Amount 0 / 0 / 1Seed 0 Applies a different random rotation to each instance. The three Amount values control variation around X, Y, and Z. The default allows free rotation around Z while keeping instances upright. This suits most plants. Add X and Y variation for objects such as rocks or debris that should tilt in several directions. Seed generates a different set of rotations. Whether Random Rotation starts enabled on new layers is determined by the add-on preferences.

Default offMax Angle 90° Restricts Random Rotation to increments of Max Angle while keeping the choice of direction random. At 90°, instances face one of four directions; at 45°, one of eight; and at 180°, one of two. Use it for objects that should retain regular alignment, such as crates, paving, or planks.

Default set in preferencesAlignment Strength 1.0 Tilts each instance to stand perpendicular to the surface beneath it. On a slope, this makes the instance lean away from vertical to match the ground. Alignment Strength blends between upright at 0 and fully surface-aligned at 1. Values around 0–0.3 are useful for trees that should remain mostly vertical. A value of 1 suits grass, rocks, and objects that should follow the ground closely.
Use a vertex group on the scatter surface to define where instances appear. The layer is kept in painted areas and excluded from unpainted areas.

Default off Enable Vertex Group and select a group from the field. Use different groups to switch between layouts such as a winding strip or isolated groves. The picker shows vertex groups from the surface the layer uses: its emitter or its Single Surface object. Mask detail depends on the surface mesh. Weights are stored per vertex. A coarse mesh produces a less detailed boundary; subdivide the relevant area when you need finer control.

Select the surface object, then click the brush button at the end of the row to enter Weight Paint mode. Paint the areas where the layer should appear. Click the button again to return to Object Mode and view the updated scatter.

Default offTransition 1.0 Without Smooth Transition, instances are either kept or excluded. With it enabled, instance scale follows the painted weight, creating smaller instances near the mask boundary. Transition sets the weight needed for full-size instances. Lower values reach full size in lightly painted areas; higher values require stronger weights.

Default off Reverses the mask so the layer appears outside the painted area. The arrow button beside the vertex group field performs the same action. For example, paint a path once, use the mask normally for gravel or flowers, and invert it on a tree layer to keep trees off the path.
Use nearby objects to exclude a layer from an area or restrict it to that area. This is useful for clear space around boulders, vegetation near walls, or plants around tree stumps.

Default offDistance 0 m Enable Geometry Proximity, choose an Object, and set Distance. With the default Avoid behaviour, instances within that distance are removed. Distance is measured from the object's surface rather than its centre, so the cleared area follows its shape.
Default offTransition 1 m Softens the boundary around the excluded area. Instances grow from zero size at the Distance boundary to full size Transition metres further away.

Default Avoid Avoid excludes instances within the specified Distance of the object. Seek keeps instances only within that Distance. Use it to concentrate vegetation around a target, such as weeds at the base of a wall or ferns around a stump.

cards.t: Type: Single Object or Multiple Objects
cards.x: Default Single Object Single Object uses one target. Multiple Objects replaces the object field with a collection picker and applies the same settings to every object in that collection.
Use a curve to define a path, road, stream, fence line, or other continuous boundary. The scatter responds when you edit the curve.
Default offDistance 1 m Enable Curve Proximity and select a Curve. With Avoid behaviour, Distance sets the clearance on each side, so use half your intended path width.
Default offTransition 2 Creates a gradual boundary along the path. Instances increase to full size over the Transition distance rather than ending abruptly.

Default off By default, distance is measured in 3D. Moving a curve far enough above the terrain can reduce or remove its effect. This can close the cleared path even though the curve has not moved sideways. Enable Infinite Z to ignore height and apply the curve's influence vertically to the terrain below. Use it to control a path on uneven terrain with a flat curve positioned above the ground.
Default Avoid Avoid clears instances along the curve. Seek keeps them only near the curve, useful for hedges, avenues of trees, or reeds beside a stream.

cards.t: Type: Single Curve or Multiple Curves
cards.x: Default Single Curve Single Curve uses one curve object. Multiple Curves uses a collection, allowing one set of proximity settings to control an entire path network.

Ecosystem settings let a layer respond to the instances of another layer. Configure them on the layer you want to control, then select the layer it should follow or avoid. For example, a bush layer can appear around the boulders in a rock layer. The target layer keeps its own settings. When its arrangement changes, such as after changing its seed, the reacting layer updates to match.

Default offDistance 0 m Enable Attraction and select the target layer under Scatter System. Instances are kept only within Distance of the target layer's instances. Lower Distance to concentrate the reacting layer into smaller patches, such as bushes close to each boulder. A Distance of 0 leaves the layer empty. Attraction starts at 0, so increase Distance after enabling it to make instances visible.
Default offTransition 1 m Softens the outer boundary of each patch. Instances remain full size up to the Distance boundary, then shrink to zero over the next Transition metres.

Default offDistance 0 m Excludes instances within Distance of the target layer and keeps them elsewhere. Use it to prevent grass from intersecting rocks or to clear small plants from the area around large trees.
Default offTransition 1 m Softens the boundary of the excluded area. Instances grow from zero size at the Distance boundary to full size Transition metres further away.

Attraction and Repulsion can be enabled together and can reference either the same layer or two different layers. When both reference the same layer, use a smaller Repulsion Distance than Attraction Distance to create a band around each target instance. For example, Attraction at 6 m and Repulsion at 3.5 m keeps bushes near boulders without placing them directly beside them. When they reference different layers, one rule attracts while the other excludes. Use this for relationships such as moss that appears near rocks but stays away from trees.
Select a group to access Group Ecosystem. Its settings apply to every layer in the group, allowing a complete planting to follow or avoid another layer together.

The Abiotic section contains three masks that control placement using the shape of the terrain. Select a layer in the System List, enable a mask, and expand it to access its settings. Each layer has its own masks, and all three can be combined. These masks hide instances by reducing their scale to zero. Smooth transitions therefore change instance size at the boundary rather than gradually reducing instance density. The Abiotic section is located between Culling and Proximity in the Scatter tab.
Restricts a layer to flatter ground, or to steeper ground when inverted. Use it to keep trees on terraces while leaving cliff faces clear.

Default 0.85Range 0 to 1 Sets the minimum flatness required to keep an instance. A value of 1 represents level ground; 0 represents a vertical wall. The layer appears on surfaces flatter than the threshold. Increase Slope to restrict placement to flatter terrain. Decrease it to allow steeper slopes. As a guide, 0.85 allows slopes of approximately 32°, 0.7 allows 45°, and 0.5 allows 60°.

Default offTransition 0.5 Blends instance size across the slope boundary. Instances have zero scale at the cutoff and reach full size where the surface is flatter by the Transition amount. A small Transition creates a narrow band of smaller instances. A larger value extends that band further onto flat ground. Keep Slope + Transition at or below 1. Surface flatness cannot exceed 1. With a higher total, instances cannot reach full size. At the defaults of 0.85 and 0.5, even level ground produces instances at 30% scale. A Transition of 0.05–0.15 is a useful starting range for most scenes.

Default off Reverses the mask, keeping the layer on steep surfaces and excluding it from flat ground. With Invert enabled, decreasing Slope restricts placement to progressively steeper surfaces. Use an inverted mask for rocks or scree on a cliff, alongside a plant layer using the same Slope value without inversion.
Restricts placement by height. Use it to create boundaries such as a mountain tree line.

Default 5 m Sets the upper height limit when Smooth Transition is disabled. Instances above the cutoff are excluded. Height is measured along the scene's Z axis in scene units. Account for the terrain's position when choosing a value, especially if it sits far above or below zero. Layer disappears after enabling the mask? The default cutoff is 5 m. If the whole emitter is above that height, increase Height until the layer becomes visible.

Default offTransition 5 Extends a scale fade above the cutoff. Instances remain full size up to Height, then shrink to zero over the next Transition metres. For example, Height at 7 m and Transition at 5 fades instances between 7 m and 12 m. Use a shorter transition for a distinct tree line or a longer one for a more gradual boundary.

Default off Keeps instances above the cutoff instead of below it. Height becomes the layer's lower boundary. Use it for high-altitude plants or rocks near a snow line. Two layers with the same Height and opposite Invert settings can divide a terrain into upper and lower regions.

Default offAmount 55Scale 0.2 Varies the height cutoff with noise so the boundary does not follow a uniform contour. Amount controls how far the cutoff can shift. At 0, it remains unchanged. The default of 55 suits large terrains; reduce it for smaller terrain where the variation would otherwise be too strong. Scale controls the frequency of the pattern. Lower values produce broad variations in the boundary; higher values produce smaller, more frequent changes.
Restricts placement according to the direction a slope faces. Use it for effects such as moss on shaded hillsides or plants on slopes facing the sun.

Default 0° Sets the compass direction the slope must face. Adjusting Angle through 360° changes the affected side of every hill. Without Smooth Transition, instance size depends on how directly the slope faces that direction. Steep surfaces facing it directly produce the largest instances, with scale tapering toward the sides. Level ground has no facing direction and remains empty at the default Offset.

Default 0 Adjusts the width of the affected region. Positive values restrict placement to steeper surfaces facing the chosen angle. Negative values extend it around the hillside and allow instances onto level ground.

Default offTransition 0.5 Controls the blend from zero to full instance scale across the mask boundary. Use a small Transition for full-size instances with a distinct edge. Larger values create a broader, softer region of reduced-scale instances. Enabling Smooth Transition slightly narrows the mask. Decrease Offset to restore the previous coverage.
Texture masks apply a pattern across the scatter surface to control where instances appear and how they scale near boundaries. Each mask has its own checkbox, and multiple masks can be combined.
Creates irregular patches with gaps between them. Use it for vegetation that should form natural clusters rather than cover the surface uniformly.

Min 0.4Max 0.6 The noise pattern has a value from 0 to 1 at each point. Instances are excluded below Min, reach full size above Max, and scale gradually between the two. Raise both thresholds to reduce coverage, or lower them to fill more of the surface. Bring the values closer for sharper boundaries; separate them for a wider scale transition.

Seed 0Scale 1.0 Seed changes the arrangement of patches while preserving the other pattern settings. Scale controls pattern frequency. Lower values create fewer, larger patches; higher values create more, smaller patches. Values around 0.1–0.3 are a useful starting point for a large terrain.

Detail 2Roughness 0.5Lacunarity 2Distortion 0 Detail adds smaller-scale patterns to the main noise. At 0, patch boundaries are smooth and rounded. Higher values create more irregular edges. Roughness sets the strength of the finer patterns. Lacunarity controls how much smaller each successive pattern becomes. Both depend on Detail being above 0. Distortion warps the noise into swirls and elongated shapes.
Creates parallel bands. Use it for crop rows, vineyards, ploughed fields, or planted borders.
Min 0.3Max 0.6 These thresholds work as they do for Noise. Increasing Min narrows the planted bands and widens the gaps. Max controls the transition to full-size instances along their edges.

Scale 0.6Phase Offset 0 Scale controls the number of rows. Lower values produce fewer, wider rows; higher values produce more, narrower rows. Phase Offset shifts the rows sideways without changing their spacing. Use it to align them with a fence, path, or another layer.

Distortion 0Detail 2Detail Scale 1Detail Roughness 0.5 Distortion bends the rows away from straight lines, creating less regular planting patterns. The other settings shape this variation and have no effect when Distortion is 0. Detail adds finer variations, Detail Scale controls their size, and Detail Roughness controls the strength of the finest changes.
Creates a rectangular grid separated by gaps. Use it for planting beds, garden plots, paving, or other regularly spaced arrangements.

Scale 2.0Gap Size 0.05 Scale controls the number of tiles. Lower values create fewer, larger tiles; higher values create more, smaller tiles. The default of 2 produces very small tiles on most surfaces, so lower it first if the pattern is difficult to see. Gap Size sets the width of the empty strips between tiles, from nearly zero to 0.125.
Width 0.5Height 0.5 Set the proportions of each tile. Equal values produce squares. Increase Width for elongated beds, or decrease Height for narrow strips.
Uses an image as the mask. White areas retain instances, and black areas exclude them. Create a mask in an image editor or use a graphic, such as a logo, to define the scatter pattern.

Default offBounds Clip Enable Image, click the folder button, and choose an image file. The layer remains empty until an image is selected. Bounds controls what happens outside the image. Clip displays it once and leaves the rest of the surface empty. Repeat tiles it across the surface. Use small instances and sufficient density for detailed shapes. Increase Density and reduce Uniform Scale if the image outline looks coarse.

Min 0Max 1Sharpen offInvert off Invert reverses the mask, filling the areas that would otherwise be empty. Min and Max control grayscale transitions. Instances are excluded below Min, full size above Max, and scaled between them. Sharpen makes soft boundaries more distinct. These three controls have little effect on a purely black-and-white image because it has no intermediate grayscale values. Use them with gradients, photographs, or softly painted masks.

Scale 1 / 1 / 1 Location moves the image across the surface in metres. Rotation changes its orientation; adjust Z to rotate it across the ground. Scale works in reverse: increasing the value makes the image smaller, while decreasing it makes the image larger. At 1, the image is approximately 10 m wide. Different X and Y values stretch the mask independently. The image retains its original aspect ratio unless you stretch it with separate axis values.
Noise, Lines, and Tiles each include transform controls for positioning and orienting their patterns.

Location moves the pattern across the surface. It shifts the mask, not the underlying instance positions. Scale stretches the pattern along individual axes. Stretching noise along X, for example, turns rounded patches into elongated bands. Rotation changes the pattern's orientation. Use Z to rotate it across the ground.
Use Rotation to set the direction of the rows. Location shifts their position, similarly to Phase Offset.
Use Location to align the grid with the surface boundaries and Rotation to change its angle.
Select a group to access Group Texture Masks. The same pattern is applied to every layer in the group, allowing them to share patches, rows, or a grid.
Dynamics controls movement over time. Play Blender's timeline to preview these effects.
Adds swaying motion to a layer's instances. Wind is disabled on new layers.

Default No Wind Wind-Performance has the lowest processing cost. It tilts and rocks each instance as a whole. Wind-Semi-Realistic adds waves of wind moving across the layer, providing a balance between motion detail and performance. Wind-Realistic bends plants along their height and adds finer flutter. It provides the most detailed motion and has the highest processing cost, indicated by a warning in the menu. Reserve it for layers that need close-up detail. Select a type to display its settings. Adjust Strength to the scale of your assets. Wind moves instances by a distance in the scene, so a value that suits a 10 m tree may bend small plants too far. Lower Strength if plants bend excessively or collapse flat.

Direction 0°Strength 2Speed 1Scale 2 Direction sets the compass direction the wind blows toward. Strength controls how far instances are pushed. Speed controls how quickly instances sway. Scale controls gust size. Lower values make larger areas move together; higher values create more variation between neighbouring instances. Wind-Performance also includes Smoothness to soften the motion.

Bending 1Minor Wind on, 1 Bending controls how much a plant curves along its height rather than tilting as a rigid object. Enable Minor Wind adds finer motion on top of the main sway. Adjust Minor Wind Strength to control its intensity. The Advanced panel contains Height Falloff and Width Falloff, which control the effect from base to tip and from centre to outer edges. A Vertex Group can limit the effect to part of the mesh.

Presets Gentle Breeze, Windy, Storm Choose a Preset and click Apply Preset to set Strength, Speed, and Scale for the selected Wind Type. Use the result as a starting point, then refine it for your assets. Gentle Breeze provides light swaying, Windy creates stronger continuous movement, and Storm produces pronounced leaning and gusts. Preset values differ between Wind Types. Apply the preset again after changing the type.

Wind is recalculated on every frame, which can slow playback on dense layers. Bake Wind stores the animation so Blender can play the cached result rather than calculate it again. In the recorded test, approximately 7,000 trees using Wind-Realistic played a 48-frame sequence at about 3 frames per second before baking and 30 frames per second afterward. The bake took 16 seconds. These figures describe that test, not a guaranteed playback speed. Choose Animation to bake the scene's full frame range, or Still to bake only the current frame. The button changes to Baked when complete. Click the bin icon to delete the bake. Save first and bake after final adjustments. Blender stores the bake beside the .blend file. Changes to wind settings, density, or the frame range require you to delete the existing bake and bake again.
Animate a layer appearing or disappearing over a frame range. Twenty presets are available, each using the same basic Animation controls.

Default No Effect Choose an effect under Preset and play the timeline. Examples include: Popup: instances appear in a wave across the layer. Radial: the layer grows outward from its centre. Vortex: instances spin down into position. Rain: instances fall into position from above. The remaining presets are Aurora Front, Ripple, Geyser, Popcorn, Corkscrew, Spinup, Jelly Pop, Card Cascade, Orbit Assemble, Shutters, Seedling Timelapse, Sun Chase, Verdant, Pop Bounce, Meteor, and Bloom.

Start Frame 1End Frame 60 to 90Reverse offSeed 0 Start Frame and End Frame define when the transition begins and when the layer is fully visible. Shorten the range to speed up the effect, or increase Start Frame to delay it. Reverse plays the transition backward, starting with the complete layer and animating it out. Seed changes the random order in which instances appear. Each preset also includes an Effect Settings panel with its own controls, such as Edge Width for Radial or Spin and Drop Height for Vortex.
Flattens instances near an object, useful for grass reacting to a ball, foot, or wheel.

Default offMin 0Max 0.2 Enable Collision and select a Collision Object. Nearby instances bend down and return to their original state when the object moves away. Max sets how far the effect reaches from the object. The default of 0.2 affects the immediate contact area. Increase it to flatten a wider area. Min defines the distance within which instances are completely flat. Between Min and Max, the flattening is partial.
Select a group to access Group Dynamics. Its settings apply to every layer in the group, allowing a complete planting to share the same motion settings.

The Materials section controls compatible materials on the layer selected in the System List. It is located at the bottom of the Scatter tab. Plants in the ScatterFlow content pack are configured for these controls. For your own assets, the available settings depend on what their materials support.

Moves the planting through Spring, Summer, Autumn, and Winter. The labels below the slider identify the seasons, while the header shows the current season and progress through it. For example, the meadow transitions from fresh spring green through pale summer straw and autumn orange to winter brown. Season Amount controls the strength of the seasonal colour adjustment. At 0, plants retain their original colours.

Seasons Blend 0.5Color Variation Blend 5Color Variation Seed 0 These controls vary the seasonal effect across the planting so every plant does not change colour together. Seasons Blend controls differences in seasonal progress between plants. Lower values produce a more uniform change; higher values let some plants appear further through the season than others. Color Variation Blend controls the size of areas that change together. Color Variation Seed rearranges those areas. Leaf Randomness adds variation between individual leaves. Season Colors sets the colours used for each season.

Default 0 Controls snow coverage on leaves. At 0, no snow is applied; at 1, the leaves are white. A value around 0.3 produces a light dusting. This setting is in the Seasons panel below Season Colors. Content pack trees also include Trunk Snow Amount for snow on their bark.

Dry Mask offSpread 0.6Scale 0.15Position 0 Creates uneven areas of dry, yellow vegetation. Set Dry Mask OFF/ON to 1 to enable the effect. Dryness Spread controls how much of the planting is affected. Dryness Scale controls patch size, and Dryness Position moves the pattern across the surface. Dry/Height Amount and Dryness Height control how far the dry colouration extends up each plant. Dryness Color sets its colour.

Stripe Scale 0.23Angle 0°Distortion 0 Creates alternating light and dark bands for a mown lawn. Lawn biomes have the effect enabled by default. Use Stripes ON/OFF to toggle it and Stripe Brightness to adjust the contrast. Stripe Scale controls band width. Angle rotates the pattern, and Position Offset shifts it sideways. Distortion makes the boundaries less regular, useful for mowing patterns that should not look perfectly straight. Stripe Spread Min and Max control the sharpness of the transition between light and dark bands.

cards.t: Material List and the link button
cards.x: The list at the top shows the ScatterFlow materials used by the selected layer. Select a material to display its Main, Translucency, and Wetness settings. These control colour adjustments, light passing through leaves, and the appearance of a wet surface. The link button beside the Materials heading applies the same adjustments to all listed materials. Unlink them to edit a material individually.

A biome combines multiple scatter layers with their assets, densities, and masks already configured. Importing a biome adds its layers to the current emitter as a group. After importing, you can adjust each layer, modify the group, or combine layers from different biomes to build your own environment.

Choose an emitter and click Open Biome Browser. Move the cursor over the editor you want to use; it highlights blue. Click to replace that editor with the browser, or press Esc or right-click to cancel. A tall area beside the viewport keeps the browser, scene, and ScatterFlow controls accessible together. Allow enough width to view multiple previews comfortably. Size adjusts preview size from 3 to 14.
Click Exit Biome Panel or the red cross beside Size. The editor returns to its previous view.

Search filters biomes by name as you type. For example, enter “meadow” to find matching biomes. Under Categories, expand ScatterFlow to browse Desert, Forest, Lawn, Meadow, Trash, Tropical, Wasteland, and Wetland. Select a category to filter the results, or choose ALL to show everything. Other installed packs have their own folders. Click a biome's star to mark it as a favourite, then select Favorites to view starred biomes. Favorites are saved between sessions. The refresh arrows beside Size reload the biome folder. Use them after installing or exporting a biome.

Click a biome's name to add all its layers to the current emitter. They arrive in a group named after the biome. For example, Forest Floor_V1 adds ten layers, including flowering plants, leaf litter, and fallen sticks. Use the group's controls to hide, duplicate, or adjust the biome as a whole. Select individual layers for more specific changes, or select the group to use Group Scattering. Importing the biome onto another emitter reuses its plants already present in the file.

Click the arrow beside a biome's name to display its Individual Layers, then click + beside the layer you want to import. Individually imported layers are not grouped. Use this to take a particular plant from a biome or combine selected layers from several biomes.

ScatterFlow estimates the number of instances before importing. If the estimate exceeds 100,000, it asks how to handle viewport density. For example, Dandelion Meadow produces approximately 115,000 instances on a 25 m square emitter. Yes, use adaptive safety imports the layers hidden in the viewport and enables Decrease Viewport Density at the displayed percentage. Render density remains unchanged. No, keep full viewport density imports the biome without these viewport reductions. Use it when your system can handle the estimated instance count. After an adaptive-safety import, enable the layers' visibility to view the biome. Adjust Viewport Density as needed to balance coverage and responsiveness. Nothing visible after importing? Adaptive safety starts layers hidden. Use each layer's monitor icon or the group's eye icon to show them. If the result looks too sparse, increase Viewport Density in Optimization.
Save your scatter setups as biomes to reuse them in other files.

Open the arrow menu below the System List buttons and choose Export Biome. The command is available when the emitter contains at least one layer. It exports every layer in that emitter's list, including its settings. Name sets the biome's display name in the Biome Browser. It initially uses the scene name. Category determines its folder in the browser's Categories list. Export Path sets the save location. The export contains a .blend file with the assets and a matching .json file describing the layers. Save them in your biomes folder to make the biome available in the browser. Preview Image optionally supplies the browser thumbnail. It is copied alongside the other files. Click OK to export. Refresh after exporting. Click the Biome Browser's refresh arrows to display the new biome.

ScatterFlow can import Graswald GScatter environments (.gscatter files) as biomes without the GScatter add-on. Imported environments become ordinary ScatterFlow layers that you can edit with ScatterFlow's controls. Download the environment, install its file once through the Content Installer, then import it from the Biome Browser whenever needed.

GScatter environments are available from the Gscatter store at store.gscatter.com. Sign in with a Graswald account and download an environment. The download is a .gscatter file, such as BeeMeadow_x441g_DryCloverField.gscatter. Each file includes the environment's scatter setup, plants, and textures. Files are often 250 MB–1 GB. Keep the original download to reinstall it or use it on another computer. Environments from other stores use the same workflow when supplied as .gscatter files. Check the licence supplied with each environment before using its assets commercially. The Biome Browser requires an environment, not a single plant. A .gscatter file containing only a plant can install successfully but has no scatter layers to display as a biome.

1. Open Edit > Preferences > Add-ons, find ScatterFlow, and expand its preferences. 2. Check Content Library Folder in the Content Installer. Use the same folder as your existing ScatterFlow content. If no folder is set, choose one with sufficient disk space; installation remains disabled until a location is selected. 3. Click Install Content Files, select the .gscatter download, and click Install ScatterFlow / GScatter Content. You can select multiple files and combine .gscatter, .zip, .rar, and .blend files in one installation. 4. Follow the status bar while installation runs. Large files are extracted in the background, leaving Blender usable. Press Esc to cancel. The completion message reports the result, for example Installed 1 content file(s): 30 new file(s), 0 existing file(s) kept. 5. Check the GScatter entry in the Content Installer. It reports the installed pack count, such as 1 pack(s). Files are extracted into ScatterFlow_GScatter\GScatterPacks within the Content Library Folder, in a subfolder named after the download. Reinstalling the same file keeps existing content and restores missing files.

Choose an emitter and open the Biome Browser. Select GScatter under Categories to display installed environments. They share one category without subcategories. Search and Favorites work as they do for other biomes. Expand an environment's Individual Layers to import selected layers with +. Each original GScatter scatter system becomes one layer; Dry Clover Field, for example, contains six. Click the environment's name to import the full setup. A progress window reports the layers being added, and the resulting layers are grouped under the environment's name. Large imports use the same instance estimate and adaptive-safety prompt as other biomes.

cards.t: What carries over, and what is approximated
cards.x: GScatter builds scatter systems from stacks of effects. ScatterFlow converts those effects to the closest available ScatterFlow settings. The result resembles the original environment but may not match it exactly. Carried over: plants and their variations, density, seed, base scale, random scale, random rotation, and surface alignment. Approximated: multiple GScatter noise masks are represented by one noise mask using the same detail and seed, with density reduced to account for the original masked areas. GScatter's percentage-based alignment becomes enabled surface alignment when the original value is at least halfway. Not imported: the GScatter terrain generator and effects without a ScatterFlow equivalent. Once imported, the layers no longer depend on GScatter. Adjust them using ScatterFlow's density, masks, slope and height rules, and other controls.

The Install button is disabled. Choose a Content Library Folder first. “GScatter package has no product.json content.” The file may not be a GScatter package, or the download may be incomplete. Download it again and compare its size with the store listing. “The selected archive is not ZIP-compatible.” The file is damaged or incomplete. Download it again. The environment is missing from the Biome Browser. Refresh the browser and select the GScatter category. Check that the Content Installer reports at least one GScatter pack and that the file contains an environment rather than a single plant. “N missing collection(s)” after importing. Required plants were not found, so their layers were skipped. Reinstall the file to restore missing content. If the environment depends on another Graswald product, install that product's .gscatter file as well. “Choose an OpenScatter emitter before importing the GScatter environment.” Select an Emitter at the top of the ScatterFlow panel. Import or viewport performance is slow. GScatter environments can be dense. Try a smaller emitter, accept adaptive safety, or reduce density on the heaviest layers. See Optimization.
These settings simplify viewport display while you work with heavy layers.

Default offViewport Density 10% Displays a percentage of the layer's instances in the viewport. At Viewport Density 10%, approximately one in ten instances is shown. Use it for dense layers such as grass, where a reduced preview is enough to evaluate placement.

Default offType Bounding Box Replaces detailed viewport meshes with simpler representations. Choose the representation under Type. Bounding Box: displays a box matching each object's bounds. Convex Hull: displays a simplified shell that follows the object's outline more closely. Proxy Object: uses a chosen mesh, such as a cone, cube, or icosphere. Select it under Proxy Object and adjust its size with Proxy Scale. Points: represents each object as a point cloud. Point Radius controls point size, and Point Density controls the number of points. Enable Bounding Box in the add-on preferences to start new layers with this optimization active.
Excludes instances outside the scene camera's view. The retained region follows the camera as it moves or rotates.

Default offWidth / Height 1.2Clip Start 5 mClip End 100 m Enable Camera Culling to restrict the layer to the camera's view and clipping range. Width and Height adjust the retained region relative to the camera frame. A value of 1 matches the frame. The default of 1.2 adds a margin to help retain instances and shadows near its edges. Clip End excludes instances beyond the specified distance. Clip Start excludes instances closer than the specified distance. Camera Culling also affects renders. Excluded instances are absent from the final render, not just the viewport. Use a generous margin, especially with a moving camera.

Default offReduction Rate 1.0Seed 0 Reduces instance density with distance from the camera. This option is part of Camera Culling. Reduction Rate controls the amount of thinning. Seed changes which instances are excluded. The effect can be subtle and is most visible in distant areas of the layer.

Default off Excludes instances hidden behind other objects from the scene camera's viewpoint. Enable the option and select a Collection containing occluding objects, such as buildings, walls, rocks, or hills. The excluded area updates as the occluding objects move. For example, moving a wall changes which trees behind it are culled. Camera Culling may also be required. In the documented tests, Occlusion Culling only affected the layer when Camera Culling was enabled. If it has no visible effect, enable Camera Culling as well.
Reduces polygon counts on the source objects in a collection. Because instances share those source meshes, the reduction applies throughout the scatter.

Expand Decimator, select the source Collection, and click Add To All to add a Decimate modifier to each object. Master Ratio sets the proportion of geometry retained across the collection. A value of 1 keeps the original detail; 0.2 keeps one fifth. The 25%, 50%, and 75% buttons provide preset ratios. Wireframe display can help you inspect the reduction. The buttons beside Global Decimation control viewport visibility, render visibility, permanent application with the checkmark, and removal with the cross. To simplify editing without reducing final detail, enable the reduction in the viewport and disable it for renders. Collection Objects lists the source objects, their polygon counts, and individual Ratio controls. Use these to retain more detail on assets that need it.

Nano is available in the ScatterFlow build of Blender. It adjusts the viewport detail of scatter instances according to their size on screen, reducing the geometry drawn for dense scenes. It works on ScatterFlow layers in Solid shading, with or without textures, and does not affect renders. The recorded comparison uses Desert_V2 on a 30 m square surface, with approximately 920,000 instances and 17 billion polygons.

The comparison shows the same scene with Nano disabled and enabled. Frame duration reflects the actual viewport redraw time, and the on-screen readout reports performance. Without Nano, redraws took approximately 1.9 seconds, or about 0.5 frames per second. With Nano enabled using the button at the right end of the viewport header, redraws took approximately 55 milliseconds, or 18 frames per second: about 35 times faster in this test. Performance depends on the scene and hardware. Treat these measurements as an example rather than an expected speedup for every project.

Click the arrow beside the Nano button to open its panel. The main button toggles Nano and displays Nano: Activated or Nano: Deactivated. Other settings are disabled while Nano is off. The enabled state is remembered between sessions. Visualizer displays diagnostic colours. Clusters shows the triangle groups used to draw each object, Detail shows the chosen detail levels, and Instances gives each instance a separate colour. Return it to Off for normal display.

Default 1 pxRange 0.25 to 8 px Sets the maximum allowed difference from the full mesh, measured on screen in pixels. Lower values retain more detail. Higher values reduce detail and improve performance. Higher values can remove fine details such as leaves, making branches more prominent. Use the Clusters visualizer to inspect how the detail changes.

Default 0 pxRange 0 to 16 px Reduces the number of instances drawn below the specified screen size. Smaller instances are reduced more strongly. At 0, all instances are drawn. Increase this value to reduce distant pebbles and small plants that contribute little visible detail.

Quick Tools are the two buttons at the top of the Scatter tab. They operate on selected mesh objects, not scatter layers, and remain disabled until a mesh is selected. After using a tool, adjust its options in Blender's Adjust Last Operation panel at the lower left of the viewport, or press F9. Changing an option immediately updates the result.
Adds variation to the scale, heading, and tilt of selected objects. Use it to make repeated props look less uniform.

Select the objects and click the button. Click again to generate another result. Each operation starts from the stored original scale and rotation rather than the previous randomized result. Repeated clicks therefore do not continually shrink or tilt the objects. Original transforms are stored for the current session. Manually scaling or rotating an object after randomizing establishes a new starting transform.

Scale Min 0.5Scale Max 1.0Max Tilt 15°Random Yaw on Scale Min and Scale Max define the random scale range. The defaults produce objects between half and full size. Set Scale Max above 1 to allow larger variations. Max Tilt sets the maximum lean away from vertical, up to 90°. Use 0 to keep objects upright. Random Yaw rotates each object randomly around its vertical axis. Disable it to preserve the original heading. Seed controls the random result. Each button click chooses a new seed; enter a specific value to reproduce a result.
Moves objects vertically until their lowest point rests on the surface beneath them. Objects above the ground move down; objects embedded in it can move up.

Select the objects and click the button. Each object is positioned on the surface beneath it. The tool changes vertical position only. It does not rotate objects to match the slope. Selected objects are excluded from one another's ground checks, so they land on the terrain rather than stacking on each other. Objects with no detected surface below them remain unchanged.

Search Distance 250 mGround Offset 0 mUse Footprint on Ground Offset adds vertical clearance. At 0, objects rest on the surface; a value of 2 m leaves a 2 m gap. Negative values embed the base slightly, useful for rocks and tree trunks. Use Footprint checks the ground below the object's centre and four corners, then uses the highest detected point to reduce sinking on slopes. Disable it to check only the centre. Search Distance sets how far below each object the tool searches for a surface.

Weather and atmosphere presets are included in the ScatterFlow content pack. Find them in the Weather and Atmosphere catalogs of the ScatterFlow_Pro_ContentPack asset library. Most effects are objects that you drag into the scene. Select the object and open the Modifier tab, identified by the blue wrench in the Properties editor, to adjust its settings. Expand the individual sections to access their controls. Rain Ripples and Rain Streaks instead use material node groups, as described below. Most effects are animated. Press Space to play the timeline and preview their movement.

1. Open Weather > Rain in the Asset Browser. Choose Drizzle, Steady Rain, or Storm as a starting intensity. 2. Drag the preset into the viewport and play the timeline. Move and scale the effect object to cover the required area. The main controls are in the RAIN section: Rain Drop Type: choose Drop for rounded drops or Line for streaks. Lines make heavy or fast rain easier to see. Rain Amount: controls rainfall density. Increase it for heavier rain or reduce it for lighter rain. RainDrop Size: sets the size of individual drops. In the Wind section, WindX and WindY push rain sideways. Adjust them to change the angle of the rainfall. Splashes adds impacts where rain hits the ground. Turbulence varies the motion, and Optimization can restrict the effect to the camera's view. Use contrast to make rain visible. Rain reads more clearly against a darker background. Reducing world lighting can also help establish an overcast appearance.

cards.t: Raindrops landing on water and wet ground
cards.x: Rain Ripples is a material node group, not a separate scene object. It adds animated impact rings to surfaces such as puddles, roads, or ponds. 1. Select the target object and open the Shader Editor. A low-Roughness material makes the ripples easier to see in reflections. 2. Open Weather > Rain in the Asset Browser and drag Rain Ripples into the Shader Editor. 3. Add a Bump node using Shift + A > Vector > Bump. 4. Connect Rain Ripples to the Bump node's Height, then connect the Bump node's Normal to the Principled BSDF's Normal input. 5. Play the timeline to preview expanding ripple rings. The Rain Ripples node includes these controls: Drop Amount: the number of raindrop impacts. Ripple Size: the width of each ring. Ripple Strength: the apparent depth of the ripples. Ripple Speed: the speed at which the rings expand. Turbulence: broader surface movement, similar to wind disturbing the water. Group Control: the overall Speed and a Randomize control for changing the pattern. Ripples too subtle? Increase the Bump node's Distance. The appropriate value depends on the surface's size in your scene.

cards.t: Water running down glass and walls
cards.x: Rain Streaks adds animated water trails and droplets to a material. Use it for windows, metal panels, glass, or wet walls. 1. Select the object and open the Shader Editor. 2. Open Weather > Rain in the Asset Browser and drag SF_RainStreaks into the Shader Editor. 3. Add a Mix Shader using Shift + A > Shader > Mix Shader, then make these connections: Connect SF_RainStreaks Mask Output to the Mix Shader's Factor. Connect the existing surface material, such as a Principled BSDF, to the first Shader input. Connect SF_RainStreaks BSDF to the second Shader input. Connect the Mix Shader output to Surface on the Material Output. 4. Play the timeline to preview water moving over the underlying material. The node includes these controls: Normal Strength, under General: how strongly the water appears raised from the surface. Bump Strength: additional surface depth for droplets. Visibility: the strength of the streaks over the original material. Scale, under Mapping: the size of the pattern. Lower values produce larger streaks. Use Location and Rotation to position and orient them. A UV map is required. Streaks use the object's UVs. If the object has no UV map, add one with UV > Smart UV Project in Edit Mode. Include a sky or lights in the scene so the water has surroundings to reflect.

1. Open Weather > Snow and drag Snowfall, Flurries, or Blizzard into the scene. 2. Position the effect above the area to cover, then play the timeline. Flakes fall from the effect object. The main controls are: Density, in the Snow section: the number of falling flakes. Increase it for heavier snowfall or reduce it for a lighter effect. Min Radius and Max Radius: the range of flake sizes. Strength, in the Wind section: how strongly wind pushes the snow. Direction sets the direction of that movement. Simulation Speed: the rate of the snowfall simulation. Accumulation controls snow buildup, Turbulence adds swirling motion, Collision allows flakes to land on selected objects, and Instance replaces the flakes with your own objects. Play from the start for accumulation. Snow buildup is calculated from the first frame. Jumping ahead can require the simulation to catch up.

Snow Cover adds settled snow to surfaces such as rocks, roofs, branches, and fences. It does not require timeline playback. 1. Place the objects that should receive snow in a collection, such as Rocks. 2. Drag Snow Cover from Weather > Snow into the scene. Its drop position does not affect which objects receive snow. 3. Expand Snow Main and select the target collection in Collission Collection. Snow appears on the objects' upper surfaces. Snow Type: choose Volume or Island. These generate the cover differently; compare them on your target objects. Snow Thickness: the depth of the cover. Smoothness: rounds the generated snow for a softer surface. Subdivision Level: adds detail at a higher processing cost. Snow Pattern adds noise to the surface. Scatter places small objects over the snow. Start with a low Subdivision Level. Detailed source objects can make Snow Cover expensive to evaluate. Increase the level only when the additional detail is needed for the final result.

These presets add bending and swaying to individual objects, such as trees or flags. For scatter layers, use Wind in the Dynamics section instead. 1. Open Weather > Wind and choose Gentle Breeze, Windy, or Storm. 2. Drag the preset onto the target object and release it over the object. 3. Play the timeline to preview the movement. The Main section contains: Wind Strength: how far the object bends. For example, compare 0.25 for gentle movement with 1.5 for stronger bending, then adjust for your asset. Direction: the wind direction. Wind Speed: how quickly gusts change. Bending: how much the upper part bends relative to the base. Wind Noise Size: the size of the gust pattern. Minor Wind adds faster, smaller movement for details such as leaves.

1. Open Atmosphere and drag Falling Leafs into the scene. 2. Play the timeline to preview falling, tumbling leaves. Menu: selects the leaf type. Options include Oak, Maple, Beech, Cherry Blossom, Willow, Lavender, Red Rose, Grass, and confetti. Count, in Spawning: how many leaves are falling at once.
