Increase it for more leaves or reduce it for a lighter effect. Scale, in Size: the size of each leaf. Tumble Speed, in Rotation: how quickly leaves rotate as they fall. In Movement, Fall Speed controls downward motion, while Sway Amount and Sway Speed control side-to-side movement. Wind Direction moves the leaves across the scene. Use Curve to guide them along a drawn path, such as a gust moving down a street.

Drag Embers from Atmosphere to the source of the effect, then play the timeline. The sparks rise and drift away. Count, in Spawning: sets the number of embers. Increase it for a fuller effect or reduce it for fewer sparks. Lifetime: how long each ember remains visible, which also affects how high it travels before fading. Movement controls upward motion and sway. Wind Direction controls their drift. Embers are easier to see against a dark environment. Lower world lighting for dusk, night, or other low-light scenes.

Dust creates small particles that drift slowly through the air. Use it as a subtle effect in sunlight, interior spaces, or other areas where airborne particles should be visible. Drag Dust from Atmosphere into the scene and play the timeline. Count, in Spawning: sets the number of dust particles. Keep it low for a subtle effect. Scale, in Size: the size of each particle. In Movement, Settle Speed controls how slowly particles sink, and Sway controls side-to-side movement. Lighting determines visibility. A strong light against a dark background, such as sunlight entering a dim room, makes dust easier to read.

Creates a localized cloud of circling gnats, suitable for areas near water or lights. 1. Drag BugSwarm from Atmosphere into the scene. The swarm forms above the drop location. 2. Play the timeline. The gnats are approximately 2 mm at their intended real-world size. They may be difficult to see from a distance; use a close camera or increase their scale. Scale: the size of the gnats. A value of 0.005 represents the life-size setup; increasing it to 0.25 makes the gnats easier to see. Count, in Spawning: the number of gnats. Increase it for a fuller swarm or reduce it for a smaller group. In Flight, Circle Radius and Circling Speed control the orbit, Attraction keeps the swarm together, and Dart Amount controls sudden movements away from the group. Match the scale to the shot. Keep the gnats small for close-up realism or enlarge them when the swarm needs to remain visible in a wider view.

Creates larger insects that flutter around a location. Use them near lamps, porches, or campfires. 1. Drag Moths from Atmosphere to the desired location. Search for “Moth” in the Asset Browser to find it. 2. Play the timeline. Count, in Spawning: the number of moths. Increase it for a larger group or reduce it for fewer moths. Scale: the size of each moth. Wing Flutter, in Rotation: the speed of the wing movement. Flight uses the same types of controls as Bug Swarm for circling, attraction, and darting. Both Bug Swarm and Moths can follow a path. Enable Use Curve Path in the Curve section and select the curve.

The Ivy tab creates climbing plants on objects such as walls, trunks, and rocks. Draw the main stems, and ScatterFlow generates vines, branches, leaves, and flowers along the surface. Use Ivy Properties to refine the result afterward.

Presets include a plant's leaves, flowers, and growth settings. The content pack provides options ranging from green climbers to flowering clematis. 1. Open an Asset Browser and select ScatterFlow_Pro_ContentPack. 2. Open Ivy > Presets. 3. Select the preset you want to use. 4. Select the target wall, click Add Ivy, and draw the stems. The new ivy uses the selected preset's assets and settings. A preset is optional. Without one, Add Ivy creates bare stems until you assign leaves. Select a preset first to start with a complete plant. If presets are missing, see Adding the library.

1. Select the target object. You can select multiple objects for the ivy to grow across. 2. Position the 3D Cursor at the plant's starting point with Shift + Right Click. 3. Click Add Ivy to activate the drawing tool. 4. Draw the main stems on the surface. Each stroke creates one stem, and you can add multiple strokes. 5. Press Tab to finish and generate the ivy. Start with a few simple strokes. The strokes define the main stems, not every vine. Branches and vines spread from them automatically, so dense drawing is often unnecessary.
Select an entry in the Ivy List and click Edit Ivy to edit its strokes. Add stems to extend coverage, or select and delete unwanted strokes. Press Tab to regenerate the plant.

Select another preset in the Asset Browser, then click Swap Preset, the circular-arrow button between Leaf Visibility and Flower Visibility. The drawn stems stay in place, while leaves, flowers, and growth settings are replaced. To replace only the leaves or flowers, use the controls described under Changing leaves and flowers.

Type Two buttons Default Realistic Mode Realistic Mode generates stems along the surface from your strokes, with attached vines, branches, leaves, and flowers. Use it when the plant will be viewed closely. Fast Mode skips the stems and covers the target with leaves and flowers. It has a lower processing cost and suits distant surfaces or large areas. The available settings depend on the mode. Switching modes changes Ivy Properties. Ivy Bake is available only in Realistic Mode.

cards.t: Leaf Visibility, Flower Visibility and the list
cards.x: Leaf Visibility and Flower Visibility toggle those parts of the selected ivy. Hide flowers for a non-flowering plant, or hide both leaves and flowers while shaping the stems. The Ivy List contains one entry per ivy in the scene. Select an entry to edit it. Each row includes: Eye: toggles viewport visibility. Camera: toggles render visibility. Bin: deletes the ivy, including its stems and collections. Hover over the i above the list for a brief workflow reminder.

The two + buttons replace leaf or flower meshes without changing the drawn stems or growth settings. The left button, beside Leaf Visibility, changes the leaves. The right button, beside Flower Visibility, changes the flowers. Replacing one does not change the other.

cards.t: Leaves and flowers from the content pack
cards.x: 1. Select the ivy in the Ivy List. 2. Open Ivy > Leafs in the Asset Browser and select a leaf set. 3. Click the left + to replace the leaves. 4. Open Ivy > Flowers, select a flower set, and click the right + to replace the flowers. You can combine sets from different plants, such as Akebia leaves and Beaumontia flowers on a clematis setup. Use the correct replacement button. Either + accepts the selected asset. A leaf set can therefore be assigned as flowers, or a flower set as leaves.

Place your leaf or flower objects in a collection. If the collection contains several objects, the ivy uses a mix of them. 1. Clear the Asset Browser selection by clicking an empty area. 2. Select your collection in the Outliner, or select an object within it. 3. Click the left + for leaves or the right + for flowers. For example, a My Leaves collection can contain multiple custom leaf shapes, while My Flowers supplies a separate flower mesh. Replacing these sources preserves the ivy's overall shape. You can also assign a collection directly in Ivy Properties: use Leaf Source in the Leafs panel or Flower Source in the Flowers panel. Asset Browser selection takes priority. If an asset remains selected there, the + button uses it instead of your selected collection. Clear the Asset Browser selection before assigning scene objects. Place origins at the attachment point. Model each leaf or flower at its intended size, with its origin where it joins the stem. Use Leaf Size, Flower Size, and rotation settings to refine its placement on the vine.
Expand Ivy Properties to access the selected plant's settings. The ivy Growth panel controls its stems and branching.

Vines Spread: how far vines extend from the drawn stems. Increase it to cover more surface without adding strokes. Branch Spread: how far smaller branches extend from the vines. Overall Vine Size: the overall stem thickness. Vines Surface Offset: the distance between stems and the target surface. Under Vines, use Vine Density for the number of vines, Vine Size for thickness, and Vine Seed for a different arrangement. Under Branches, Branch Density, Branch Size, and Branch Seed provide equivalent controls for branches. Leaves and flowers grow on branches, so increasing branch density produces a fuller plant. Use seeds to try different growth patterns. Changing a seed preserves the other settings while regenerating the arrangement. This is useful when a vine grows into an unwanted position.

Fast Mode has no drawn stems to edit. Its ivy Growth panel instead provides: Spread: coverage distance across the target, in metres. Density: the amount of surface coverage. Max Scale and Min Scale: the random size range for the generated pieces. Seed: a different arrangement using the same settings. The Leafs, Flowers, Wind, and Optimization panels are available in both modes.

The Leafs checkbox toggles leaves, like Leaf Visibility. Leaf Source selects the collection used for their meshes. Leaf Density: the number of leaves along the stems. Leaf Spacing: the minimum gap between leaves. Leaf Seed: a different arrangement using the same leaf sources. Leaf Size Min and Leaf Size Max: the range of leaf sizes. Leaf Rotation and Leaf Rotation2: random rotation amounts. Leaf Downward Tilt Min and Max: the range of downward leaf tilt.

The Flowers panel follows the same pattern as Leafs: the Flowers checkbox enables them, Flower Source selects their collection, and Flower Density, Flower Spacing, Flower Seed, Flower Size Min, and Max control their placement and variation. Under Flower Rotation, Flowers Rotation adds random rotation. Flowers Min and Max Upward Tilt control how far flowers face upward and away from the surface. Adjust Flower Density gradually. Presets use values around 0.01; a value of 0.05 can already produce dense flowering.

Enable Wind and play the timeline to preview leaf and flower movement. Global/Wind Strength: how far the leaves and flowers move. Global/Wind Speed: how quickly the leaves and flowers move. Global/Wind Scale: the gust size. Smaller values create variation between neighbouring leaves; larger values make broader areas move together. Keep ivy wind subtle. Use low strength to move the leaves without making the whole plant appear to sway away from the wall.

Viewport Density: the proportion of leaves and flowers shown in the viewport, from 0 to 1. Lower it to keep a heavy scene responsive while editing. Viewport Level and Render Level: how many times growth expands from itself. Higher levels produce substantially more coverage and require more processing. Separate values let you work at viewport level 1 while rendering a more detailed plant. Under Advanced, Decimate Vines and Decimate Branches simplify the stems, while Vines Resolution controls their roundness. Higher decimation values reduce processing cost but also change the growth pattern, so set them before refining the plant. Increase levels one step at a time. Level 3 can generate a very dense plant on a large wall.
Misc contains finer controls for stem variation, including Noise Scale, Noise Strength, and Branch Offset. Sources identifies the drawn curve, target objects, and Vines Material used for the stems.

Ivy updates when something it depends on changes. Baking stores the finished plant to improve playback in heavy scenes. The bake controls are at the bottom of Ivy Properties in Realistic Mode. Still: caches the current frame. Use it for ivy without animation. Animation: caches the full scene frame range, including wind. Bake Ivy: starts the bake. Bin: deletes the cache so the ivy can respond to edits again. Save before baking, and bake after final edits. A baked ivy does not respond to setting changes until you delete its bake.

The River tab creates a river from a stroke drawn on terrain. ScatterFlow shapes the riverbed in the terrain, adds animated water, and can scatter rocks or other assets along its banks. The result remains editable. Change the course, width, water settings, or bank scatter as your scene develops.

1. Select the terrain. 2. Click Draw River to activate the drawing tool. 3. Draw the river's course across the terrain in one stroke. 4. Press Tab to finish and generate the river. The terrain's name appears beside River System at the top of the panel. Hover over the i for a summary of the workflow. Prepare the terrain first. Apply its scale and rotation with Ctrl + A and provide enough geometry to shape the riverbed. A coarse terrain mesh produces rough banks and a less detailed channel.
Click Edit River to modify the strokes. Add another stroke to create a tributary, or select and delete strokes you no longer need. Press Tab to update the river.

Water follows the direction of the drawn stroke, from its starting point to its endpoint. Reverse the stroke when the flow runs the wrong way; you do not need to redraw the river. 1. Click Edit River. 2. Select the stroke to reverse. Press A for all strokes, or hover over one and press L to select it. 3. Right-click and choose Switch Direction, also available in the viewport header's Segments menu. 4. Press Tab to apply the change. The river keeps its course and flows in the opposite direction. Increase Flow Speed temporarily if you need to make the direction easier to inspect.
Open River Properties > River > Size.

cards.t: River Width, River Height and Terrain Falloff
cards.x: River Width: the width of the river. River Height: the water level within the riverbed. Raising it fills more of the channel and increases the area covered by water. Terrain Falloff: how far terrain reshaping extends from the river. Lower values create steeper banks; higher values produce a broader, gentler valley. Control Curves, at the top of the River panel, identifies the collection containing the drawn strokes.
These controls shape the animated water surface. Play the timeline to preview the result. Solid shading makes the surface geometry easier to inspect without the water material.

Wave Strength: wave height. For example, increasing it from 0.07 to 0.5 changes a calm stream into visibly rougher water. Wave Speed: how quickly the waves change. Flow Speed: how fast the water moves downstream. Flow Strength: the strength of the streaking along the flow direction. Foam Spread: how far foam extends from banks and objects in the water. See Foam. Separate motion adjustments from material adjustments. Use Solid shading to tune waves and ripples, then switch to Material Preview or Rendered shading to evaluate the water's appearance.

Add collision objects to create disturbances around rocks or other objects in the river. 1. Put the objects in a collection, such as River Boulders. 2. Expand Extra Collision Objects and select the collection in Collider. The Water panel contains two controls for these disturbances: Collision Ripples Strength: how high the ripples are. Increase it for more pronounced ripples around collision objects. Collision Ripples Falloff: the distance the ripples extend from each object. Increasing it from 0.1 m to 1 m spreads the effect over a wider area.

The river includes a separate scatter system for assets that should follow its course, such as rocks, pebbles, or reeds. Scatter Collection: the source objects. For example, use Temperate Rocks from the content pack. Scatter Amount: the number of instances placed. Min Distance: the minimum spacing between instances. Scatter Width: how far placement extends from the river. Lower values concentrate assets near the water; higher values spread them further up the banks. Scatter Falloff: how quickly coverage decreases toward the edge of the scatter band. Seed: a different arrangement with the same settings. Scale: Uniform Scale adjusts all instances, while Scale Min and Scale Max define random size variation. Rotation: Align To Surface follows the terrain slope, while Rotation and Random Rotation control orientation. Offset: shifts the scattered instances, for example to embed them slightly in the ground. Foam around scattered objects requires Realize All Instances. Keep this enabled when you need that interaction. It increases processing cost, so use a modest Scatter Amount while editing a long river.
Open SF_River Material below River Properties to adjust the water's appearance. These changes are visible in Material Preview and Rendered shading.

Water Color: the water tint. Use it to change the overall colour, such as from the pale default to blue. Water Density: how quickly colour builds through the water. Lower values produce lighter, clearer water; higher values produce a darker, deeper appearance. Murkiness Color and Water Murkiness: add a cloudy tint that obscures the bottom. A brown tint can create muddy water. Wave Bump adds fine surface detail with Scale, Detail, Distance, and Strength. Depth controls darkening in deeper areas.

Foam appears along the banks and around objects in the water. Foam Color and Foam Amount: its colour and coverage. Foam Scale and Foam Detail: the size and complexity of its pattern. Foam Bump Strength and Foam Bump Distance: the apparent surface depth of the foam. Caustics adds moving light patterns in shallow water. Adjust them with Caustic Amount, Caustic Strength, Caustic Speed, and Caustic Scale.
River tools and ordinary scatter layers can use the same terrain. The layers follow the reshaped ground, but do not automatically avoid the water.

cards.t: Scattering on a terrain with a river
cards.x: Use the terrain as the Emitter and create layers normally. Instances follow the riverbed and banks because the river modifies the terrain itself. Without a mask, the layer also scatters inside the channel. Use Curve Proximity to keep vegetation out of the water. Use the appropriate scatter system. The river's Scatter System handles assets that belong in or near the water. Use ordinary scatter layers for the rest of the terrain.

cards.t: Keep a layer out of the river with Curve Proximity
cards.x: The river's control curve can also define an exclusion area for scatter layers. 1. Select the layer in the System List and expand Proximity. 2. Enable Curve Proximity and keep Type set to Single Curve. 3. Set Curve to SF_River Curve, located in the Outliner's SF_RiverCurves collection. 4. Keep Behaviour set to Avoid and increase Distance until the channel is clear. Distance is measured from the river's centreline, so use at least half the river width. Add more clearance to keep plants off wet banks. 5. Enable Smooth Transition and adjust Transition to create a gradual boundary along the water. Repeat this for every layer that should avoid the river. Tributaries added with Edit River remain part of the same curve and are included automatically. For a second, separate river, use Multiple Curves and select a collection containing both curves. See Culling and Proximity for more detail on these controls.

River Resolution: the detail of the generated river geometry. Lower it to reduce processing cost on long rivers. Subdivide Level: adds geometry to the terrain around the river, from 0 to 6. Increase it when banks appear blocky and you cannot add detail to the terrain mesh directly. Each additional level increases the processing cost substantially.

The Decals tab adds an image as a separate object on a surface. Use decals for road markings, signs, cracks, dirt, or other localized details. Each decal remains editable after placement. You can move it, resize it, change its appearance, or hide it without modifying the underlying surface material.

cards.t: Choose an image, then place it
cards.x: 1. Click + beside Decal Objects to open the file browser. 2. Select an image and click Add New Decal. Supported formats are PNG, JPG, TIFF, EXR, TGA, and WebP. Images with transparent backgrounds provide clean outlines around the visible artwork. 3. Move the cursor over the target surface. The preview arrow shows the placement position and orientation. Left-click to confirm the position. 4. Move the mouse vertically to set the size, then left-click. 5. Move the mouse horizontally to set the rotation, then left-click to finish. The lower-left corner of the viewport shows the current step. Press Esc or right-click to cancel. Decals preserve the image's proportions. A wide image produces a wide decal. The decal faces outward from the surface where it is placed, including walls, floors, and rocks.

cards.t: A decal with normal and roughness maps
cards.x: Select multiple texture maps for the same material with Ctrl-click in the file browser. ScatterFlow connects them to the decal automatically, allowing effects such as a rust stain with colour, normal, and roughness detail. Map types are identified by their filename endings: _color, _albedo, _diffuse, or _basecolor: colour. _n, _nrm, or _normal: normal. _rough or _roughness: roughness. _metal or _metallic: metallic. _alpha, _opacity, or _mask: transparency. _emit or _emissive: emission. Map not recognized? Rename it using one of the supported endings above.

The list contains every decal in the scene, named after its image. Select a row to display that decal's settings in Decal Properties. Arrow: selects the decal in the viewport so you can move it with G. Eye: toggles visibility in both the viewport and renders.

Click the magnet button below + to enable Surface Snap. While active, moving a decal with G keeps it attached to the surface under the cursor and aligns it to face outward. Use it to move a decal between differently oriented surfaces, such as from the ground onto a wall, without manually adjusting its rotation. Surface Snap also affects other objects. It enables Blender's face snapping. Click the magnet again when finished to avoid snapping other objects unintentionally.
Select a decal and expand Decal Properties. Its target surface is shown at the top.

Opacity: how visible the decal is over the surface. Lower it for faded or worn markings. Emission: adds glow for details such as illuminated signs or screens. Metallic and Roughness: adjust the surface appearance. Low Roughness produces sharper reflections suitable for stickers or wet paint. Alpha: the transparency supplied by the image.

cards.t: Color Adjustment, Damage, Dirt and Blur
cards.x: Color Adjustment: Hue shifts colours, with 0.5 leaving them unchanged. Saturation controls colour intensity, and Value controls brightness. Use these to recolor a decal without editing its source image. Damage: removes areas of the decal for a chipped or peeling appearance. Damage Amount is sensitive: values from 0.01 to 0.04 range from small chips to substantial removal. Scale controls chip size, while Detail, Roughness, and Lacunarity shape their edges. Damage Position shifts the pattern. Dirt: adds a grime tint. Dirt Amount and Dirt Color set its strength and colour, while Wetness and Bump control gloss and apparent surface depth. The effect can be subtle on small decals. Blur: softens the image. At 1, it becomes a diffuse patch, useful for faint stains or shadow-like details.

The Physics tab uses simulated falling and collisions to place objects. Use it for arrangements such as rolling barrels, stacked tyres, or rocks settled into corners that would be time-consuming to position individually. You can add physics to existing objects or place new objects with brushes that simulate them as you work.
Placement brushes use objects from a Source Collection in the current file.

Source Collection: selects the available assets. For example, a Debris collection can contain barrels, tyres, and rocks. Arrow: expands the collection's object list. Tick boxes: enable or exclude individual objects from new placements. Disable an asset temporarily without removing it from the collection. All and None: enable or disable every listed object. +: adds selected scene objects or Asset Browser assets to the source collection. Keep the source objects in the scene. The brushes place copies of them. Move the originals out of the camera's view rather than deleting them.
These four controls apply to selected objects, including objects you have positioned manually.

Set Passive: makes objects participate in collisions without moving. Apply it to the ground, walls, ramps, and other supporting surfaces before dropping objects onto them. Add Physics: enables simulated falling and collisions on the selection. Apply it to the objects you want to move, then play the timeline. Objects falling through the floor? Select the floor and apply Set Passive so it can receive collisions.

Freeze: holds selected objects at their current positions while keeping them solid for collisions. Use Freeze to lock a completed part of a pile before adding more objects. Newly dropped objects can still land on the frozen ones. Remove: removes physics and leaves the objects at their settled positions as ordinary scene objects.
The placement brushes are called modes. They use the Source Collection and simulate objects live without requiring timeline playback.

Click Start Scattering to display six mode dials on the left of the viewport. The button changes to Stop Scattering while the controls are active. Click a mode or press its number, 1–6, to display its settings. A shortcut card appears in the lower-left corner. Drag a setting dial horizontally to adjust it. Click an On/Off dial to toggle it. Press Esc or right-click to leave the active mode and return to the mode list. Press Esc again, or click Stop Scattering, to close the controls. The modes are Area, Precision, Push, Array, Grab, and Move.
Hold the left mouse button to place objects within the brush circle. Objects continue spawning while the button is held.

Hold the cursor in one place to build a pile, or drag to distribute objects along a path. They fall and settle as they are added. Use short presses for controlled placement. A long press can generate many objects quickly.
Sets the number of objects added at each brush step. For example, Count 6 adds six objects per step instead of one at Count 1, producing a denser result over the same press duration.
Sets the area within which objects appear. A radius of 0.6 creates a compact pile, while 2.5 spreads the same number over a wider region. Hold F and move the mouse to adjust it interactively.
Define the random size range. Set both to 1 to preserve every source object's size. A range of 0.4–2.0 produces a mix of smaller and larger copies.

Sets how far above the target surface objects spawn. At 0 they are placed at the ground; a value of 4 drops them from above, allowing more falling, bouncing, and rolling before they settle. Align to Surface tilts the brush circle to match the surface beneath it.
When disabled, objects spawn upright. Enable it to start each object at a random orientation, allowing it to settle on a different side or end.
Hold Ctrl and drag to remove objects under the brush. Randomize generates a new variation for objects placed by the brushes. Randomize Selected limits that action to the current selection.

Click to place one object under the cursor. Q, or the Next Asset dial, selects the next object in the Source Collection. Shift + click places another copy of the same object. Scale Min, Scale Max, Height Offset, Align to Surface, and Random Rotation work as they do in Area mode. Skip Rigid Body places objects without physics. They remain where you put them, including when Height Offset places them above the ground. Hold Ctrl and drag to erase. Use F to adjust the eraser radius.
Use these modes to rearrange objects already placed in the scene.

Hold the left mouse button and drag to move a plane through the objects, pushing them like a broom. Push Width sets the plane's width. A value of 0.8 affects a narrow strip; 3.0 covers a broader area. Hold F and move the mouse to adjust it.

Hold the left mouse button to pull objects inside the brush toward its centre. Drag to carry them together, useful for gathering scattered objects into a pile. Grab Radius sets the affected area. Strength: negative values attract objects.

Positive Strength pushes objects away from the brush centre. Increase it gradually for a stronger push rather than starting with a large value. Damping reduces object motion. Lower values allow objects to travel further after being pushed. Adjust Strength gradually. High positive values can throw objects a long distance.
Click and drag an object to reposition it. Release the mouse button to return it to the simulation at its new location.

Array repeats one object in a regular pattern, such as stacked crates, a pallet of blocks, or a ring of tyres. Its settings appear in the sidebar under Modes rather than on dials. 1. Select the source object and choose Array. 2. Click Add Array. Array Type: choose Grid for rows and stacks or Radial for rings. Count: Grid uses X Count, Y Count, and Z Count. Radial uses Radial Count around each ring, Radial Rings for the number of rings, and Z Count for vertical layers. Spacing: sets the gaps along each grid axis. Radial arrangements use Ring Spacing and Start Radius. Scale: Base Scale sets overall size, while Random Scale Min and Max add variation. Rotation: Base Rotation sets the starting orientation, and Random Rotation adds variation. Advanced: Realize Instances converts the generated instances into geometry.

ScatterFlow organizes physics objects into collections listed under Sources, with a count for each: Quick Spawn: objects placed with the brushes. Active Rigid Bodies: objects assigned physics with Add Physics. Passive Rigid Bodies: objects assigned Set Passive, such as the ground. Frozen Objects: objects held in place with Freeze. Arrow: selects every object in the collection for actions such as Freeze, Remove, or Randomize Selected. Eye: toggles collection visibility.

cards.t: From loose objects to a scatter layer
cards.x: Convert to Scatter replaces placed objects with instances in a layer named Physics Scatter. It preserves their positions, rotations, and scales while reducing the overhead of many separate objects. 1. Select an Emitter in the Scatter tab. The new layer needs an emitter to belong to. 2. Click Convert to Scatter and confirm. Physics Scatter appears in the System List as a Manual layer. You can continue refining its instances with the Manual Mode brushes. To convert only part of the arrangement, select those objects before running the command. Conversion ends their physics simulation. Finish settling and rearranging the objects before converting them.

Control how objects respond when they contact one another. Collision Type: the shape used for collision calculations. Convex Hull approximates the outer shape and suits many objects. Box, Sphere, Capsule, and Cylinder are simpler options with lower processing cost. Mesh follows the surface more closely, useful for hollow objects that other objects need to enter. Friction: resistance to sliding. Lower values allow surfaces to slide more freely. Bounce: how strongly objects rebound after contact. Increase it for more bounce or reduce it for less. Collision Margin: an additional collision boundary around the object. Rolling and Spinning: resistance to those types of motion. Increase Rolling to help barrels settle rather than continue rolling. Friction Anchor: helps stabilize stacks that gradually slide apart. Set as Default: uses the current values for objects assigned physics afterward. Apply to Selected: applies the values to selected objects. Contact behaviour depends on both surfaces. Apply Bounce and Friction settings to the ground as well as to falling objects.

cards.t: Split Impulse, PyBullet Solver and Origin Tools
cards.x: Split Impulse reduces the tendency of initially overlapping objects to be pushed violently apart. Leave Enable Split Impulse enabled. Rigid Body Cache defines the frame range for timeline-based simulation. PyBullet Solver balances accuracy and processing cost. Increase Iterations and Substeps when small or fast objects pass through surfaces or stacks remain unstable. Other solver controls provide finer adjustments for difficult contacts. Origin Tools: Center of Mass (Vol) moves object origins to their volume-based centre of mass for more natural tumbling. Bottom Center places origins at the centre of each base for easier surface placement.

ScatterFlow connects Blender directly to an open Unreal Engine or Godot project. Once connected, you can export supported scene content without manually exporting files and importing them in the engine. The export handles two main types of content: Objects, such as rocks, buildings, and terrain meshes, arrive with their materials. Scatter layers arrive as editable ScatterFlow layers rather than thousands of separate objects. You can continue adjusting them in the engine. Re-exporting updates existing content rather than creating duplicates. ScatterFlow tracks what has already been sent and updates changed content.

cards.t: Pick the engine and click Connect
cards.x: 1. Open the project in the engine with the ScatterFlow plugin enabled. In Unreal, click ScatterFlow in the main toolbar beside the Play controls. In Godot, open the ScatterFlow Pro dock. 2. Select Unreal or Godot at the top of Blender's Export tab. 3. Click Connect. The status indicator shows the connection state: Red, Not Connected: Blender has not connected to the engine. Orange, Connecting…: a connection is being established. Green, Connected to Unreal: the connection is ready for export. Click Disconnect before switching to another engine. Connection remains red? Check that the engine plugin is running. Then compare Link URL in Blender's ScatterFlow preferences under Export with the address shown in the engine's ScatterFlow panel.

cards.t: Tick what you want to export
cards.x: The two checkboxes under Export determine which content the export includes. Selected Objects: exports objects selected in the viewport. The accompanying count distinguishes new objects, such as “2 new,” from “tracked” objects that have been sent before and can be updated. Scatter System: exports enabled scatter layers. The count reports the number selected, such as “3 of 3.” Use the checkboxes in Scatter Layers to choose individual layers. All enables every layer; None disables them all. Excluding a layer does not delete it from the engine. It simply skips that layer's update. Exclude unchanged layers to reduce export work.

Click Export to Unreal or Export to Godot. The button displays Exporting… until the operation finishes. Selected objects and enabled scatter layers can be sent in the same export. For example, export two manually placed boulders together with three scatter layers. Continue editing in Blender and export again to update the engine. Previously exported objects are updated in place rather than duplicated.
Click Settings beside the Export title to access optional export controls. The defaults provide a starting setup for most scenes.

For objects Materials: includes the object's materials. Disable it when you intend to build the materials in the engine yourself. Collision: adds collision so characters can stand on surfaces and are blocked by solid objects. Nanite (Unreal only): enables Unreal's Nanite for exported objects, useful for detailed meshes. For scatter layers Emitter: includes the terrain used by the layers. Disable it when the terrain is already in the engine and only the layers need updating. Nanite (Unreal only): enables Nanite for the terrain and scattered assets. PCG Mode: sets the layer's initial behaviour in the engine. Exact Mode preserves Blender's instance positions. Procedural Mode lets the engine regenerate the scatter so you can adjust density and distribution there. You can change modes later in the engine.

cards.t: What is sent, and what is not
cards.s: What is sent, and what is not
cards.x: Export supports the content listed below. Other parts of the environment need to be recreated or configured in the destination engine.

cards.s: What is sent, and what is not
cards.x: Selected mesh objects, with materials and optional collision. Materials are baked when required, as described under Texture Baking. Previously exported objects update in place. Lights, except sun lamps. Collection instances, represented in Blender by an Empty that instances a collection, arrive with the collection's meshes and share one mesh per source object. ScatterFlow scatter layers, including their instances. Layers above 1,000,000 instances, or 500,000 for Godot, use a stream file that the engine loads around the camera. Ivy and water bodies created with ScatterFlow. Blender objects configured to be visible only in shadows, with Camera off and Shadow on under Object Properties > Visibility, remain shadow-only in the engine. Objects disabled for rendering arrive hidden.

cards.t: Not sent: set these up in the engine
cards.s: What is sent, and what is not
cards.x: The World: sky, HDRI, sky light, exposure, and view transform. Configure these in the engine, or use ScatterFlow Sky in Unreal. Sun lamps and fog boxes: use the engine's sun and fog setup. Weather: enable rain and snow through the engine's ScatterFlow controls. Rivers: water bodies are supported, but river systems are not exported.

cards.s: What is sent, and what is not
cards.x: Only ScatterFlow layers are transferred as scatter systems. Particle systems, other Geometry Nodes setups, and instances from other scattering tools are excluded. Convert them to real objects or bring them into ScatterFlow first. For GScatter environments, use the import workflow described under Biomes. OpenVDB volume objects are also excluded and are reported in the export log.

Blender material node setups do not always translate directly to the engine's material setup. ScatterFlow converts unsupported combinations, such as procedural textures, colour ramps, or mixed shaders, into image textures before export. This process is called baking. Expand Texture Baking below the Export button. Its header shows the current behaviour: Auto, Bake All, or Off. Bake on Export if not PBR: bakes only materials that require conversion. This is enabled by default and suits most scenes. Bake All: bakes every material, including image-based materials. Use it when a transferred material differs from its Blender appearance. Resolution: sets baked texture size. Source matches the source images. Select 2K or 4K for higher resolution, with larger output files. Samples: increase this if baked textures appear grainy. Timeout per Pass (min): limits the time allowed for one bake pass, such as Base Color on one object. If it exceeds the limit, the object is exported without baking. See When a bake is skipped or fails. Initial exports can take longer. Baking runs during export. Later exports reuse cached images when the relevant inputs have not changed.
This section explains how ScatterFlow decides what to bake, stores the results, and handles material features that cannot be preserved in a static texture.

A material consisting of image textures connected to a Principled BSDF can be transferred without baking. The engine rebuilds its supported material inputs from those textures. Baking is used when the material cannot be reconstructed that way, including setups with: procedural textures such as Noise, Voronoi, Musgrave, Wave, or Brick; Color Ramps; Mix Shaders; shaders other than Principled BSDF, such as Diffuse, Glossy, or Translucent; or node groups that modify their inputs. Two kinds of setup can bypass baking despite including additional nodes: Simple image adjustments, including Mapping-node tiling or offset, colour tinting, brightness or contrast changes, and roughness remapping. The texture and supported adjustments are transferred for the engine to apply. Inactive operations, such as a Mix at factor 0, a Bump at strength 0, muted nodes, or groups with zero influence. ScatterFlow follows the active result through these nodes and exports the underlying textures.

ScatterFlow uses Cycles to bake material channels into separate images. Channels include Base Color, Roughness, Metallic, Specular, Opacity, and Normal, plus Translucency and Emission when present. Bump and normal-map inputs are combined into the baked normal map. Baking uses a temporary copy of the object with its modifiers applied, in a separate background Blender process. Your active Blender session remains usable, and the scene's scatter is not loaded into the bake process. A failure in that process does not close the active session. The viewport progress card shows the current object and pass; press Esc to cancel. The bake uses the GPU configured in Blender's Preferences > System, or the CPU when no GPU is configured. You can select the device under ScatterFlow's Preferences > Export > Texture Baking > Device. The panel reports when no GPU is set up.

Images are cached in _BakeCache inside the export's Sync Folder, which is next to the .blend file by default. Re-exports reuse them unless the material, mesh UVs, or bake settings have changed. Materials that depend only on UVs, including image mixes, ramps, colour adjustments, and normal maps, can share one bake across objects. For example, tree variants using the same UV-based leaf material reuse that material's baked textures. Delete _BakeCache before exporting to force a complete rebake.

cards.t: Ground materials that blend two textures
cards.x: A terrain material may blend two tiling texture sets, such as grass and dirt, using a mask. Baking the whole terrain into one image can lose detail; for example, a 2K texture stretched across 100 m provides limited surface resolution. ScatterFlow instead bakes each texture set as a tile and exports the blend mask separately. The engine tiles and blends the results. This requires each set to use one Mapping node without rotation, the first UV map, and no dependence on position or normals.

Baking uses the object's first UV map, matching the map used by the engine. Coordinates outside the 0–1 range are wrapped back into that range for baking, matching repeated textures such as tiled bark or planks. UDIM materials are baked into a single image, causing their tiles to overlap. The export log warns when this occurs.
Nested groups are supported, but some material effects depend on information that cannot be stored in a static image. The following sections describe the resulting limitations.

cards.t: Node groups, nested groups and layered shaders
cards.x: The bake follows connections through node groups and nested groups. You do not need to ungroup a material before exporting. Layered materials, such as rock, moss, and dirt blended with masks, are baked using their combined result. Material Outputs inside groups, including those used by some vegetation assets, are also detected.

cards.t: Nodes that depend on the camera or the lighting
cards.x: Fresnel, Layer Weight, Light Path, Camera Data, and Ambient Occlusion can depend on the view or lighting. A bake captures a fixed result, so these baked effects do not continue responding to the camera in the engine. Glass transparency driven by Fresnel or Layer Weight is a supported exception: ScatterFlow rebuilds it using the engine's Fresnel behaviour instead of baking the transparency effect.

cards.t: Variation per copy or over time
cards.x: Per-object variation: values from Object Info, such as Random or Location, or Particle Info can produce different colours for each copy in Blender. A baked image is shared by copies of the mesh, so this variation is not retained in the shared texture. Use separate mesh variants or the engine's per-instance variation controls. Animation: time- or frame-driven material values are baked at the current frame. The resulting texture does not preserve the animation.

Displacement: Material Output displacement does not deform the exported engine mesh. Procedural displacement is baked into the normal map as apparent surface detail rather than geometry. An image height map connected to Material Output does not trigger baking by itself. Volume shaders: not baked. Configure fog and other volume effects in the engine. Rain ripples and wetness: ScatterFlow weather additions are excluded from material baking. The engine's weather system provides these effects live rather than fixing one animated state into a texture.

cards.t: When a bake is skipped or fails
cards.s: When a bake is skipped or fails
cards.x: A bake failure does not stop the export. The affected material is sent with its available textures and values instead. After export, the status bar summarizes the result, for example 12 material(s) baked, 1 mesh(es) skipped: Rock_03 (see Info log). The Info editor lists skipped objects and their reasons. For detailed bake output, open Window > Toggle System Console.

cards.s: When a bake is skipped or fails
cards.x: The object has no UV map for the baked image. Its procedural materials are exported without baking. Fix: select the object, enter Edit Mode with Tab, select all geometry, and use UV > Smart UV Project. Export again.

cards.s: When a bake is skipped or fails
cards.x: The first UV map contains invalid values, potentially from an import or modifier. Fix: unwrap the object again with UV > Smart UV Project or Unwrap. If a modifier creates the UVs, apply it and inspect the result in the UV Editor.

cards.s: When a bake is skipped or fails
cards.x: A pass exceeded Timeout per Pass. Baking stops for that object, and it is exported without the baked result. Fix: increase Timeout per Pass when more processing time is needed. Dense meshes, 4K output, high Samples, and CPU baking can all increase bake time.

cards.s: When a bake is skipped or fails
cards.x: GPU not configured: check Edit > Preferences > System > Cycles Render Devices. Configure a GPU rather than relying on CPU baking when appropriate for your setup. Bake settings: Samples 4 is sufficient for most materials in this workflow. Source resolution preserves the size of existing textures. A 4K bake can take approximately four times as long as a 2K bake. First export: materials that require baking have no cached results yet. Subsequent exports bake only changed content.

cards.s: When a bake is skipped or fails
cards.x: An image used by the material is missing, often after moving a scene between computers. ScatterFlow searches beside the .blend file and in its textures folder, and checks for another loaded copy. Fix: use File > External Data > Find Missing Files, select the folder containing the textures, and export again.

cards.t: Grainy, blurry or different from Blender
cards.s: When a bake is skipped or fails
cards.x: Grainy: increase Samples. Blurry: increase Resolution. Source uses the largest image in the material, or 1K for fully procedural materials. Different appearance: enable Bake All to bake rather than reconstruct the material from its textures. If differences remain, check the limitations under Complicated materials and node groups.

cards.t: An object is not baked at all
cards.s: When a bake is skipped or fails
cards.x: Only mesh objects are baked. Curves, text, and other object types are exported without baking their materials. Fix: convert the object with Object > Convert > Mesh. Use a copy when you need to preserve the editable original.

Player Preview lets you inspect the Blender scene from a player's viewpoint before exporting. It does not require a running engine or connection. 1. Position the viewport at the starting location. 2. Click Preview under Player Preview. 3. Navigate using the controls shown on the shortcut card: W A S D moves, the mouse looks around, Shift runs, Space jumps, and Ctrl crouches. V cycles between first-person, third-person, and top-down views. The mouse wheel adjusts camera distance in third-person and top-down views. Hold the right mouse button to zoom. H hides the shortcut card. Esc ends the preview and restores the previous viewport. Use the different views to inspect placement, scene scale, and how the environment reads while moving through it. Open Settings below Preview to choose the starting camera and location, use the current viewport or 3D Cursor, enable full screen, adjust movement speeds and mouse sensitivity, or enable collision with scattered objects.

Preview updates run up to 60 times per second and account for elapsed time, keeping movement speed consistent at rates such as 60 or 25 frames per second. Each update accounts for at most one twentieth of a second. Below 20 frames per second, movement slows: at 10 frames per second it runs at half speed, and at 5 it runs at a quarter speed. Improve viewport performance rather than trying to compensate with Walk Speed. What makes a scene slow to draw Scatter density: large instance counts. Reduce Viewport Density or use Nano; see Optimization. These viewport changes preserve full render density. Complex meshes: detailed assets repeated many times. Use lighter meshes or proxies during editing. Modifiers: Subdivision Surface, Geometry Nodes, and other modifiers requiring recalculation. Animation: armatures, drivers, simulations, animated objects, and wind. Shading: demanding materials, lights, or textures in Material Preview or Rendered shading. Other applications: an open game engine or another 3D application shares GPU resources. Preview settings: enable Fullscreen Preview and leave Collide with Scattered Objects disabled for scenes with large instance counts.

The ScatterFlow plugin adds a panel to the Unreal Editor for scene transfer, scatter editing, and environment tools. Connect Blender and Unreal. Export supported content from Blender's ScatterFlow Export tab directly into the open level, without manually importing files. Edit scatter layers in Unreal. Each Blender scatter layer arrives as one ScatterFlow actor containing its instances. Select it to adjust density, scale, meshes, or procedural placement without returning to Blender. Add environment tools. Configure foliage wind, a dynamic sky, weather, water, and ivy. Use Play to explore the level with a supplied character.
The plugin requires Unreal Engine 5.8 on Windows, an Unreal project, and ScatterFlow for Blender. Install it separately in each project's Plugins folder.

1. Close the project in the Unreal Editor. 2. Extract ScatterFlow_UnrealPlugin_V1.0.zip, which contains ScatterFlowUnrealSync. Use a short extraction path such as C:\Temp to avoid Windows path-length problems with long filenames. 3. Open the project folder containing the .uproject file. Create a Plugins folder beside it if one does not exist. 4. Move ScatterFlowUnrealSync into Plugins. Confirm that Plugins\ScatterFlowUnrealSync\ScatterFlowUnrealSync.uplugin exists. Avoid an extra nested ScatterFlowUnrealSync folder. 5. Open the project. The plugin is precompiled for Unreal 5.8 on Windows. Its dependencies—PCG, WebSocket Networking, and Procedural Mesh Component—are enabled as part of the setup. 6. Open Edit > Plugins, search for ScatterFlow, and confirm that ScatterFlow Unreal Sync is enabled. It is marked Beta. If you enable it here, click Restart Now. 7. Confirm that the ScatterFlow button appears in the main toolbar, then continue to Step 1.

Close Unreal, delete the existing Plugins\ScatterFlowUnrealSync folder, and replace it with the new version using steps 2–4. Remove the old folder first so obsolete files are not left behind. Update the Blender add-on at the same time to keep both sides on the same release.

cards.t: If the plugin does not load
cards.x: Modules are missing or were built for another engine version. This plugin build supports Unreal Engine 5.8. Other engine versions are not supported by this build. The ScatterFlow toolbar button is missing. Confirm that the plugin is enabled and that its folder is not nested an extra level deep. Blender cannot connect. Both applications must be open. Check that Blender's connection address matches the plugin's Link Settings; see Step 2.

Click ScatterFlow in the main toolbar beside the Play controls to open the panel. It is also available from Tools > ScatterFlow Scatter. The panel opens in a floating window. Move and resize it to fit your workspace; it can remain open while you edit the level. At the top of the panel: Play starts a walkthrough using the ScatterFlow character. See Play. The connection status displays Blender connected with a green indicator when the link is active. Link Settings opens the Blender connection settings. The editing line identifies the active selection. With no layer selected, it reads Select a layer to edit it and displays the scene tools. The four icons add water, ivy, weather, or sky. The panel follows your selection. Select a ScatterFlow layer to edit its settings. Click empty space to return to the scene tools.
The plugin starts its connection service with Unreal. In Blender's Export tab, select Unreal and click Connect. When connected, the Unreal panel reports Blender connected.

Click Link Settings to view the connection controls. The defaults normally require no changes. The status line shows the current state, such as Connected — ready. Its tag is CONNECTED, LISTENING while waiting for Blender, or OFFLINE when stopped. Blender connection URL: the address Blender connects to. It must match the Unreal Link URL in Blender's ScatterFlow preferences. Use Copy URL after changing the port to update Blender's address. Port: the connection's network port. Change it only when another application is using the same port. Stop the link first; this field is disabled while it is running. Start with Unreal: starts the connection service when the project opens. Leave it enabled for normal use. Auto-import scatter exports from Blender: also detects scatter exports saved to disk while the connection was inactive. Exports sent over an active connection arrive regardless of this option. Live sync edits to Blender: sends changes to linked objects back to Blender as you edit them in Unreal. Mirror deletes to Blender: also deletes the linked Blender object when you delete it in Unreal. This is disabled by default to avoid unintended deletion of Blender content. Stop Live Link: stops the connection service.

Click an option's checkbox to enable or disable it. Changes take effect immediately and are retained when you reopen the project. Enable deletion syncing deliberately. Live sync is useful when refining placement in Unreal, but keep Mirror deletes to Blender disabled unless deletions should also affect the Blender scene.

Stop Live Link closes the connection and changes the status to Blender link offline. Start Live Link opens the service again. The status changes to Waiting for Blender until a connection is established. Blender does not reconnect automatically. Click Connect in its Export tab again to restore the link.
Once connected, click Export to Unreal in Blender. Supported content is added to the level currently open in Unreal. See Export for selection and export options.

Unreal creates the incoming assets and places the exported scene content in the level. The Outliner identifies the resulting actors. For a meadow with three scatter layers and two selected boulders, these include: SF Terrain - Meadow: the scatter terrain as a mesh with its material and collision. SF Scatter - Trees, SF Scatter - Bushes, and SF Scatter - Rocks: one actor per scatter layer, containing that layer's instances. Boulder 1 and Boulder 2: the individually selected Blender objects. Subsequent exports update the existing actors instead of adding duplicates. Layer settings can retain Unreal-side edits. On re-export, settings changed in Blender replace their corresponding values; unchanged Blender settings leave Unreal adjustments intact. See Scatter Layers for the separate behaviour of the mesh list.

cards.t: Select a layer to edit it
cards.x: Click an instance in the viewport to select its entire layer. The panel displays that layer's controls, with a label such as Editing Trees. Ctrl+click an instance from another layer to edit both together. The label changes to Editing 2 layers, and adjustments apply to both. Click empty space to deselect and return to the scene tools.

Select actors in the level, expand Export, and click Export to Blender. Actors originally exported from Blender update their existing Blender objects. Meshes created in Unreal arrive as new Blender meshes with their materials. Use this to transfer an engine-created prop, such as a crate, into the Blender scene.

Enable Live sync edits to Blender in Link Settings to send edits to linked actors immediately, without manually exporting each change. For example, repositioning a linked crate in Unreal also updates its position in Blender.
Modified settings display a round-arrow button labeled Reset to the value from Blender. Click it to restore that setting's imported value.

Use the two mode buttons to choose how the layer is placed. Blender Exact preserves the instance positions exported from Blender. Use it when placement must match the original, especially for manually arranged layers. Procedural regenerates the scatter in Unreal using its PCG system. It provides density, spacing, and mask controls, and lets the layer respond to changes in the ground. The panel displays the settings available for the selected mode. You can switch back to Blender Exact to return to the imported placement.

These controls modify the imported instances without generating a new layout. Z Offset (cm): moves every instance vertically. Positive values raise it; negative values embed it in the ground. Use it to correct floating bases or exposed roots. Keep Ratio (thinning): sets the proportion retained. A value of 1 keeps every instance, while 0.5 keeps half at random. Use it to reduce density without regenerating positions.

Expand Scale to access the size controls. Scale Multiplier: scales all instances relative to their Blender sizes. A value of 1 leaves them unchanged. Random Scale Min and Random Scale Max: add a random scale factor between the two values. Set both to 1 for no additional variation.

Rotation X / Y / Z (deg): rotates all instances by the specified angles. Use X or Y to lean a layer and Z to change its heading. Random Spin (+/- deg): adds random rotation around each instance's up axis, within the specified angle in either direction.

The Meshes section lists each source mesh, such as Mesh 1 and Mesh 2, with its instance count. Use the controls beside a mesh to replace it or locate its asset: 1. Click the mesh name to open the asset picker. Search for and select a replacement. 2. Select a mesh in the Content Browser or Content Drawer, then click the arrow beside the mesh name to assign it. 3. Click the folder button to locate the current mesh in the Content Browser. This does not replace it. Replacing a source mesh updates every instance that uses that slot. Re-exporting replaces the mesh list. The next Blender export restores Blender's list. Make lasting source-mesh changes in Blender.

In Procedural mode, you can add meshes to the layer: Add Mesh: opens the asset picker and adds the chosen mesh. Add Selected from Content Browser: adds all selected static meshes from the Content Browser or Content Drawer. Weight: controls how often a mesh is selected relative to others. For example, set a bush's weight to 3 and a rock's to 1 to use the bush three times as often. Meshes added in Unreal have an x button for removal. Meshes imported from Blender cannot be removed here.

Ctrl+click instances or layer actors in the Outliner to select multiple layers. The panel reports the number selected, such as Editing 2 layers, and changes apply to all of them. Use this to adjust the scale of trees and bushes together, then reset the modified settings when comparing results.

Regenerate: recalculates placement using the current ground. Use it after sculpting a Landscape or changing a surface's collision. Select in Level: selects the layer actors in the level and Outliner. Open PCG Graph: opens the graph Unreal uses to generate the layer. This is intended for users who need to inspect or work with the underlying PCG setup.
These controls appear in Procedural mode. Changing a setting regenerates the layer and updates the viewport.

cards.t: Surface: what the layer grows on
cards.x: Terrain + Landscape is the default. It restricts placement to the layer's imported terrain and Unreal Landscapes, leaving objects on top of the terrain clear. Any Geometry allows placement on geometry beneath the scatter points. Use Any Geometry when assets should also cover surfaces such as roofs or boulders. Return to Terrain + Landscape to keep those surfaces excluded.

To add one specific object as a surface without allowing all geometry: 1. Select the target object, such as a boulder. 2. Ctrl+click an instance from the layer so both the object and layer are selected. 3. Expand Surface and click Use Selected Actor as Surface. The selected object receives instances while unrelated objects remain excluded.

Z Offset (cm) raises or lowers all instances. Use small positive values for bases that sit too low, or negative values to embed them slightly. Inspect the result from ground level to judge contact with the surface.

Use a top-down view to evaluate changes in coverage and spacing. Density / m²: the number of instances per square metre, initially taken from Blender. Increasing it from 0.03 to 0.15 multiplies the base density by five. Density Multiplier: scales the density without replacing the base value. Use it to compare denser or sparser versions of the layer.
Changes the random layout while retaining the other settings and instance count. Try different seeds to adjust the arrangement without rebuilding the setup.

Min Distance (cm) sets the minimum spacing between instances. Instances that are too close to one another are removed. Increase it to reduce clustering and produce more even spacing. Higher values can reduce the final count even when Density remains unchanged.
Uniform Scale: adjusts the size of every instance. Non-Uniform: scales X, Y, and Z independently. Use Z to change height and X or Y to change width.

Enable Random Scale to assign each instance a factor between Min Scale and Max Scale, multiplied by Uniform Scale. Wider ranges create stronger size variation; 0.4–2.0, for example, mixes substantially smaller and larger trees.

Use a hillside, such as a 30° slope, to inspect alignment clearly. Align to Surface: makes instances stand perpendicular to the ground beneath them. This suits rocks, grass, and ground cover. Leave it disabled for trees that should remain vertical on slopes. Range X / Y / Z (deg): the X and Y controls add random tilt up to the specified angles. Values around 5–15° can break up uniformly upright placement.

Enable Random Rotation to vary instance orientation and reduce visible repetition. Disable it to preserve matching orientations. The Z value in Range X / Y / Z limits the heading variation. At 360°, instances can face any direction. Lower values restrict the range; 0 removes the variation.
Masks restrict procedural placement to selected parts of the surface. Each has an Enabled control, and Invert reverses its affected region. Masks are available in Procedural mode.

Use this mask to keep vegetation on flatter ground or restrict assets to steep surfaces. Max Slope: the steepest allowed surface angle, in degrees. Lowering it from 76 to 15 clears steep banks while retaining flatter terraces. Falloff (deg): softens the transition at the slope boundary. Invert: reverses the mask to keep instances on steep ground instead of flat areas.

Use this mask for height-based boundaries such as a tree line. Height (cm): the upper placement limit. On a 10 m hill, changing the limit between 1.5 m and 7 m substantially changes the covered area; enter the corresponding values in centimetres. Falloff (cm): the height range over which the layer fades at the boundary. Invert: keeps instances above the height limit instead of below it.

Breaks the layer into irregular patches rather than uniform coverage. Scale (lower = bigger patches): controls pattern size. Decrease it for broader patches. Threshold Min and Threshold Max: control coverage and the transition between patches and gaps. A wider interval creates softer boundaries. Detail: adds finer irregularity to patch edges. Seed: rearranges the pattern without changing its other settings. Invert: exchanges the populated areas and gaps.

Restricts placement around target objects, such as keeping plants away from a house. 1. Select the target object, then Ctrl+click an instance to include the layer in the selection. 2. Click Add Selected under Geometry Proximity. The object is added to the list and the mask is enabled. 3. Set Distance (cm) to define the affected area around the object. 4. Set Transition (cm) to soften the boundary. 5. Choose Behaviour: Repel excludes nearby instances, while Attract keeps instances only near the target. Click an object's x to remove it. Clear removes all targets added in Unreal. Targets imported from Blender remain and are counted separately above the list.

Uses a spline to define a path, road, river margin, or other continuous region. 1. Select the layer and click Draw New Spline. A short, selected spline appears where the viewport is looking. 2. Shape the spline by moving its points. Alt+drag an endpoint to add more points. 3. Select the layer again and set Distance (cm). With Repel behaviour, this clears the specified distance on each side of the spline. At 0, nothing is cleared; 400 creates 4 m of clearance per side. 4. Adjust Transition (cm) to soften the outer boundaries. 5. Choose Behaviour: Attract keeps instances along the spline, while Repel clears them away from it. To use an existing actor with a Spline component, select it together with the layer and click Add Selected under Curve Proximity. Editing the spline updates the scatter when you release the point.

Deselect any layer and expand Wind to configure the level-wide effect. This wind drives ScatterFlow plants, rain, snow, water waves, and ivy. Enabled: toggles wind. Strength: controls how far plants bend. Speed: controls how quickly they sway. Direction (deg): sets the direction the wind blows toward. Gustiness: varies the wind in gusts rather than maintaining a steady effect. Leaf Flutter: adds faster, smaller leaf movement over the main sway. Realtime viewport required. Enable Realtime in the viewport to preview wind animation. It is enabled by default.

Select a layer and expand its Wind section. These controls multiply the level-wide wind values for that layer. Layer Wind Strength: 0 disables motion for the layer, useful for rocks or rigid assets. A value of 2 doubles its response. Layer Wind Speed: adjusts the layer's motion speed relative to the level's wind.

Position the viewport at the intended starting location and click Play at the top of the panel. The ScatterFlow character starts on the ground beneath the viewport camera. No separate game mode or character setup is required. The on-screen card lists the controls: W A S D to move, mouse to look, hold Shift to sprint, Space to jump, C to crouch, and V to switch between first- and third-person views. Hold the right mouse button to zoom, use Shift+F1 to release the mouse, and press H to hide the card. Click Stop in the panel to end the preview.

Character: selects a custom character Blueprint. Leave it at None to use the supplied ScatterFlow character. Start at Editor Camera: starts beneath the viewport camera. Disable it to use the level's Player Start. Apply These Settings: applies the camera and movement values below. Disable it to keep the character's own settings. Show Controls While Playing: toggles the shortcut card. Third-Person Camera: adjust Distance, Side Offset, and Height Offset to position the camera. Field of View controls the normal view, and Zoom FOV applies while holding the right mouse button. Camera Lag and its speed control how the camera follows movement. First-Person Eye Height sets the height used after switching views with V. Movement: configure Walk Speed, Crouch Speed, Jump Strength, Gravity Scale, and Air Control, which determines steering while airborne. Crouch Animation and Sprint: choose the animations and stride length per loop to reduce foot sliding. ScatterFlow supplies these animations, or you can assign the character's own versions.
Adjust the camera before starting Play. Increase Distance to follow further behind the character, and raise Height Offset for a higher viewpoint.

ScatterFlow Sky combines the sun, moon, stars, volumetric clouds, fog, and exposure in one actor. It also responds to ScatterFlow weather, adjusting cloud cover and lighting for rain or snow. Add the sky from the panel, then use its Sky section to configure the environment.

Deselect any layer and click the sun icon beside Select a layer to edit it. On first use, ScatterFlow creates the required materials and textures. The sky is then added and its settings open. Existing sun, sky light, atmosphere, clouds, fog, and sky dome actors are disabled to avoid overlapping sky systems. Remove Sky restores them. Enable Realtime to preview cloud movement. The setting is available in the viewport menu.

Time sets the hour. Drag the value or enter a time such as 6:30 PM or 18.5. Changing it updates the sun's position, sky colour, lighting, shadows, and cloud illumination. The sky transitions through dawn, daylight, sunset, twilight, and night, with the moon and stars visible after dark.

Rotates the sun's path around the scene, changing where it rises and sets without changing the time of day. The moon and stars rotate with it. Use it to choose the direction of the lighting and shadows independently of the time setting.

Sets the latitude used by the sky, affecting sun height, day length, and twilight. Adjust it to change the sun's path through the scene. Watch the sun and shadows while adjusting Latitude to judge the change in lighting.

cards.t: Animate While Playing and Day Length
cards.x: Animate While Playing: advances time during gameplay. Disable it to keep the selected time fixed. Day Length (min): the real-time duration of a complete day cycle. A value of 2 produces a fast cycle useful for previewing changes from afternoon to sunset.
Choose Clear, Partly Cloudy, Cloudy, Overcast, or Foggy to set clouds, lighting, and fog together. These presets describe dry conditions; configure precipitation on the Weather page.

Density: cloud thickness and opacity. Lower values allow more light through; higher values create denser clouds with darker interiors. Scale: cloud size. Lower values create smaller formations, while higher values create broader clouds.
Sets the height of the cloud layer's underside in kilometres. Lower clouds appear closer and occupy more of the view; higher clouds appear further away.
Sets cloud movement in metres per second. At 0, clouds stop drifting. They move in the direction of the level's wind.
Enables moving shadows from clouds on the terrain. Disable it to remove their influence on direct lighting below.

Controls sunlight strength. Automatic exposure compensates for lighting changes, so increasing intensity does not necessarily brighten the entire image. It can instead produce stronger contrast and more pronounced shadows.
Controls distance haze. Higher values obscure distant objects first and progressively affect nearer areas. The fog colour follows the sky and sun.

Allows sunlight to illuminate the fog itself, creating visible light and depth in the atmosphere. It is especially apparent with a low sun shining through the haze. This option is disabled by default because it adds rendering cost.

Moon Intensity (lux): moonlight strength. A value of 0 produces very dark nights; increase it to improve nighttime visibility. Stars: the brightness of the stars and Milky Way. They become visible after sunset and are obscured by clouds.

Select Sky: selects the sky actor so you can access its full Details panel. Additional controls include day and night length, day of year, moon phase, cloud colours, and exposure. Remove Sky: deletes the ScatterFlow sky and restores the level's previous sky setup.

ScatterFlow Weather creates rain or snow around the camera and applies wetness, puddles, or snow cover across scene materials without configuring each material individually. When ScatterFlow Sky is present, it responds to the weather: rain darkens the lighting and increases cloud cover, snow adds pale clouds and haze, and thunderstorms add lightning.

Click the rain-cloud icon beside Select a layer to edit it to start rain. On first use, ScatterFlow builds the required weather assets. Choose None in the Weather section to stop precipitation and return the sky to its Sky Preset.

Choose None, Light Rain, Rain, Thunderstorm, Light Snow, Snow, or Blizzard. Each preset configures precipitation, surface effects, and sky conditions together. Start with the closest preset, then refine it. The visible controls change with the selected weather: rain settings for rain and snow settings for snow.

Controls how strongly the weather changes the sky. At 1, the normal weather response is applied. At 0, precipitation continues without changing the fair-weather sky. A value of 2 intensifies the sky response. At 0, cloud coverage comes from Fair Weather Clouds in the Sky section's Clouds panel. This defines the dry-sky conditions before and after the weather.

Transition (s) sets how long a weather change takes during gameplay. In the editor, changes normally appear immediately. For example, an 8-second transition gradually increases cloud cover and surface wetness when switching to Rain. Selecting None transitions back to dry conditions.

Use a dark background to inspect raindrop shape and visibility. Opacity: drop visibility. Drop Width and Drop Length: the dimensions of the rain streaks. Fall Speed: how quickly drops descend. Lower values produce slower motion. Particle Count: the number of drops around the camera at full intensity, up to 100,000. Intensity: overall rainfall strength, affecting both falling drops and surface wetness.
Controls how strongly precipitation follows the level's Wind. At 0, rain and snow fall vertically regardless of wind. A value of 2 doubles the directional response.
Splashes adds small crown-shaped impacts where raindrops hit the ground. Disabling it removes these impacts but leaves puddle ripple rings. Splash Amount controls their number.

Wet Surfaces: enables darker, glossier surfaces and puddles in flat areas without editing the underlying materials. Disable it to keep the ground dry while rain continues. Darkening: how much wet surfaces darken. At 0, wetness changes gloss without darkening; at 1, the surface has a strongly soaked appearance.
Puddles controls water coverage on flat ground. At 0, no puddles appear. Increase it to create larger pools.

Puddle waves add wind-driven surface motion. To inspect them separately, temporarily disable falling rain and impact rings and view reflections at a low angle. Puddle Waves: wave strength. At 0, the surface remains still; higher values disturb the reflections. Wave Scale: the size of the waves, from smaller ripples to broader swells. Wave Speed: how quickly waves move. At 0, their motion stops.
Controls the rings created by raindrop impacts. At 0, the rings are disabled. Increase it for a stronger effect. Disable puddle waves when you need to inspect the rings on their own.

Flake Size: the size of individual flakes. Fall Speed: how quickly snowflakes fall. Increase it for faster, heavier-looking snowfall. Drift: swirling motion during descent. At 0, flakes fall straight down. Particle Count and Opacity: the number and visibility of flakes.

Snow Cover: applies settled snow to upward-facing surfaces. Disable it to show falling snow without accumulation on the environment. Max Coverage: the proportion covered. Lower values leave patches; 1 creates full coverage.
Sets the steepest surface that can retain snow. Lower values remove snow from steep hillsides while preserving it on flatter areas.

Use partial coverage, such as Max Coverage 0.35, to expose the patch pattern. Cover Noise Scale: patch frequency. Lower values create broader drifts; higher values create smaller patches. Cover Edge Detail: boundary irregularity. At 0, edges are smooth; higher values add fine detail.

Dry Under Cover: excludes precipitation, wetness, and snow beneath roofs, bridges, and dense tree cover. Disable it to apply weather effects in those areas as well. Cover Area: the distance around the camera over which shelter is evaluated, in centimetres. Shelters beyond this range are not included.
Enabled by default, this shows the completed weather state immediately in the editor. Disable it to preview the gradual changes used during gameplay, such as wet ground slowly becoming snow-covered.
Add lakes, ponds, oceans, or pools with animated waves, depth-based colour, caustics, foam, and underwater effects. Start with a preset, then adjust it to suit the environment.

Point the viewport at the target location and click the water-drop icon. A flat water body is created and selected, displaying its settings. Move it to the intended water level so it intersects the terrain. Shoreline foam and depth colouration appear where the ground meets the water, allowing low areas of the terrain to form a lake. Use Add Water in the Water section to create additional water bodies.
Lake, Pond, Ocean, Tropical, Pool, and Swamp configure colour, waves, ripples, caustics, and foam together. Applying a preset preserves the water body's size and position.

Water Color: the colour of deep water. Click the swatch to change it. Clarity: the visibility distance through the water in centimetres, before its colour obscures the view. Turbidity: the cloudy appearance of the water. At 0, it is clear and dark; at 1, it is milky. Refraction: how strongly waves distort the view beneath the surface.

Wave Height and Wave Length: the height and spacing of large waves, in centimetres. Wave Speed: the speed of wave movement. Choppiness: the shape of the crests, from rounded swells at 0 to sharper peaks at 1. Wave Direction: the direction waves travel. Follow Wind: uses the level's wind direction for wave travel.
Ripple Strength, Ripple Size, and Ripple Speed: the smaller-scale surface movement. Caustic Strength, Caustic Size, and Caustic Speed: the moving light patterns beneath the water.
Shore Foam and Shore Foam Width: foam in shallow areas and around objects intersecting the water. Crest Foam: foam on steep wave crests. Increase wave height first when evaluating this effect.

Underwater Look: enables coloured haze, light shafts, and caustics when the camera is below the surface. Underwater Fog: haze density. A value of 1 matches the Clarity setting used above the surface. Light Shafts: sunlight rays visible through the water.

Affects Character: enables water interaction during Play. Wading slows movement, water carries the character, deeper water provides flotation, and movement creates surface ripples. Wade Drag: the strength of the slowdown, reaching its full effect at waist depth. Character Ripples: the strength of the rings and foam created by movement through the water. Use Play to test the transition from walking on land to wading or floating, then back onto the shore.
Generate climbing ivy over walls, rocks, trees, or ground surfaces. Adjust growth, leaves, and flowers from the panel, and use blockers to keep selected areas clear.
